items.title: ODRO’S Foundation supports persons living with disabilities in Cape Coast
items.description: ODRO’S Foundation has continued its 16-year commitment to supporting persons living with disabilities in Cape Coast by distributing mobility aids, assistive devices, and educational support materials to promote independence, dignity, and inclusion. The 2026 intervention comprises 13 wheelchairs, two walkers, four crutches, one pair of callipers, 30 spare wheelchair tyres, 20 walking-stick rubber tips, 20 mattresses and 20 “chopboxes,” as they are locally referred to. The mattresses and chopboxes are intended to support children with disabilities pursuing Senior High School education by providing essential items that make their time away from home more comfortable and manageable. Chief Executive Officer of the Office of the Registrar of Companies (ORC), Maame Samma Peprah, who has joined her father in sustaining the initiative, said the support was about more than providing physical items. “For us, this is about dignity, independence and ensuring that persons living with disabilities have the opportunity to participate fully in society. “A wheelchair, a pair of crutches or even a mattress for a student may seem like a simple item, but for the beneficiary, it can make a significant difference in their daily life and ability to pursue their aspirations,” she said. She added that the continued support reflected a commitment to ensuring that persons living with disabilities, particularly young people, were not excluded from opportunities in education and community life. “We are proud to continue what started 16 years ago, but we also recognise that the work must continue. Inclusion requires sustained commitment, partnerships and a willingness to respond to the actual needs of people,” Mrs Peprah said. The initiative traces its roots to Victoria Park in Cape Coast in 2010, when members of the disability community participating in sporting activities appealed for assistance to acquire equipment that would enable them to participate more fully in sports and community life. That request set in motion a partnership involving Albert Barton Odro, Principal Lecturer in Mental Health Studies at Middlesex University in London; his neighbour in the United Kingdom, Mr Nesad Causevic, a specialist in wheelchair engineering; and Alhaji Meffle, former Regional Manager of NITA Central and former patron of persons with disabilities, who has served as Chairman of the initiative since its inception. Through Mr Causevic’s support, wheelchairs no longer required by users in the UK were sourced, collected and shipped to Ghana, with the first major consignment comprising 13 wheelchairs and 100 spare wheels for repairs and maintenance. What began as a response to a request at Victoria Park has since evolved into an enduring partnership focused on improving mobility, education and the general wellbeing of persons living with disabilities. The initiative has been sustained through the contributions of the Odro family and its longstanding partners, with ODRO’S FOUNDATION continuing the work by expanding support beyond mobility equipment to include educational and other essential items. The foundation says the 2026 intervention reflects its broader commitment to inclusion, dignity, independence and equal opportunity, particularly for persons who face barriers to education, mobility and participation in community life. The support is intended not only to meet immediate needs but also to help beneficiaries pursue their education and participate more fully in society. With the latest distribution, ODRO’S Foundation is reaffirming a commitment that began with a simple appeal at Victoria Park in 2010. Sixteen years later, the initiative continues to bring together family, longstanding partners and members of the disability community in a shared effort to ensure that persons living with disabilities are supported to live with greater dignity, independence and opportunity.

items.title: Lutte contre les catastrophes : La FONGTO outille les partenaires du projet RPR-Togo sur les risques climatiques
items.description: Lomé, 9 sept. (ATOP) – Un atelier de formation s’est ouvert, le mercredi 9 septembre à Lomé, sur les changements climatiques et l’action anticipatoire, à l’intention des cadres de Plan international Togo, des membres de la Plateforme nationale de Réduction des risques de catastrophes et des organisations de la société civile. Cette rencontre, de trois jours, est organisée par la Fédération des organisations non gouvernementales au Togo (FONGTO) avec l’appui financier de Plan International Togo. Elle s’inscrit dans le cadre de la mise en œuvre du projet « Répondre, Protéger, Reconstruire » (RPR-Togo). L’objectif est de renforcer les capacités du personnel de Plan International Togo et des organisations partenaires sur les changements climatiques et l’action anticipatoire, afin d’améliorer la préparation, la résilience et la qualité des interventions humanitaires et de développement. Il s’agit également de renforcer les connaissances des participants sur les changements climatiques et leurs impacts, d’améliorer leurs capacités d’analyse des risques climatiques et des vulnérabilités, ainsi que de renforcer leurs compétences sur les principes et les mécanismes de l’action anticipatoire. Des participants Les participants seront outillés sur des modules, entre autres, les aspects généraux sur le contexte climatique à l’échelle globale, régionale et nationale; les généralités sur Finance climat; le focus sur Fond Vert pour le Climat, Fond d ’Adaptation et Fond pour les pertes et préjudices. L’assistance suivra aussi des présentations sur les principes et mécanismes de l’action anticipatoire; le cadre de gestion des risques et catastrophes et le Système d’alerte précoce (SAP). Le président par intérim du Conseil d’administration de la FONGTO, Hansan Ametepe, a souligné la recrudescence des aléas météorologiques extrêmes au Togo et l’urgence de changer de paradigme. « Il ne suffit plus d’attendre qu’une catastrophe survienne pour intervenir. Nous devons mieux anticiper les risques, mieux nous préparer et agir suffisamment tôt pour réduire leurs conséquences. C’est tout le sens de l’action anticipatoire », a-t-il déclaré. M. Ametepe a rappelé que cet atelier prolonge les actions concrètes déjà menées par le projet RPR-Togo, notamment l’appui à l’Agence nationale de la protection civile (ANPC) lors de l’exercice national de simulation « MIA DZRADO 2026 » dans le Bas-Mono, ainsi que la remise officielle de douze motopompes à l’ANPC en juillet dernier. Le directeur du Développement de programme et d’influence Plan international Togo, Abdoul-Baki Labodja a indiqué que Plan International Togo intègre dans sa stratégie la gestion des urgences, particulièrement dans les Savanes. Il a souligné qu’afin d’aligner le niveau de préparation et d’intervention de ses partenaires face aux aléas climatiques, l’organisation a mobilisé un financement nordique. Les travaux connaissent la participation d’experts et de représentants du Programme des Nations unies pour le développement (PNUD), de l’Organisation des nations unies pour l’alimentation et l’agriculture (FAO), de la Croix-Rouge Togolaise et de l’ANPC, concrétisant la synergie requise entre institutions publiques et société civile face aux défis climatiques. ATOP/SED/MD

items.title: Chelsea fight back from 2-0 down to beat Leeds 6-3
items.description: Chelsea fought back from two goals down to beat Leeds 6-3 as Cole Palmer and Danny Welbeck rescued the Blues in a League Cup third-round classic on Wednesday. Xabi Alonso’s side were in danger of crashing out following Tarik Muharemovic’s first-half opener and a Brenden Aaronson goal soon after the interval at Stamford Bridge. But Alonso sent on England forward Palmer, along with Morgan Rogers, Pedro Neto and Reece James, at half-time and the decision inspired Chelsea’s stirring escape act. Palmer struck twice to haul Chelsea level and Neto put them ahead before Welbeck made it four. Dominic Calvert-Lewin got one back for Leeds, but Valentin Barco and Welbeck netted to ensure Chelsea moved into the fourth round in style. Losing 2-1 at Premier League champions Arsenal on Sunday had ended Alonso’s three-game winning start to his reign. But the Chelsea boss got back on track with the kind of chaotic victory that has defined his brief spell in charge. Chelsea have scored 16 goals in Alonso’s first five matches to showcase their attacking talent. But they have conceded 10 to prove the defensive issues that plagued them last season have not gone away since Alonso’s arrival. Despite spending £349 million ($472 million) during the transfer window, Chelsea ended the Arsenal game with James and Malo Gusto — two players who are usually right-backs — operating in central midfield. Alonso fielded another untested alignment in the midfield engine room as teenage debut Reggie Watson lined up alongside Argentine youngster Barco. The 16-year-old Watson — the fourth youngest player in Chelsea’s history — is the son of Ben Watson, who scored Wigan’s FA Cup final winner against Manchester City in 2013. Alonso’s decision to make nine changes was in danger of backfiring when Leeds went in front from a 23rd-minute corner. – Chelsea goal spree – Harry Wilson’s delivery to the far post caught Chelsea flat-footed and Bosnia defender Muharemovic powered a header past Mike Penders for his first Leeds goal. Leeds seemed unfazed by the introduction of Chelsea’s stars at the interval and they struck again in the 48th minute. Ethan Ampadu’s cross was flicked on by Lukas Nmecha and Aaronson finished with aplomb. But Chelsea earned a crucial lifeline five minutes later when Daniel James’s soft challenge on Pep Chavarria was deemed worthy of a penalty that Palmer stroked home. Just two minutes later, Chelsea were level when Palmer’s shot trickled past Leeds’ debutant goalkeeper Michael Zetterer. Suddenly, Chelsea were rampant and Neto curled their third goal beyond Zetterer from 20 yards in the 60th minute. Alonso’s men made it four goals in the space of just 12 minutes as Welbeck turned and smashed a powerful strike past Zetterer’s weak attempted save. Calvert-Lewin reduced the deficit in the 75th minute with a clinical finish from Noah Okafor’s pass. But Barco swept into the empty net after Zetterer made a hash of Rogers’s cross in the 80th minute. And Welbeck rounded off the goal spree in stoppage time with a cushioned header from Barco’s shot. League Cup holders Manchester City and Premier League champions Arsenal play their third-round ties next week against Norwich and Ipswich respectively. Liverpool, who host Tottenham, and Manchester United, who welcome Brighton to Old Trafford, are also in action next week. Newcastle, Crystal Palace, Bournemouth, Sunderland and Bradford all advanced to the fourth round on Tuesday. items.title: Éliminatoires CAN 2027 : Sénégal-Mozambique délocalisé à Maputo
items.description: Le Sénégal ne recevra finalement pas le Mozambique à Dakar. Prévue initialement au stade Léopold Sédar Senghor, le 25 septembre prochain, la rencontre comptant pour les éliminatoires de la CAN 2027 se jouera finalement au Mozambique, au Stade national Zimpeto de Maputo. Coup de théâtre dans la programmation des prochaines journées des éliminatoires de la Coupe d’Afrique des nations 2027. Alors que la Fédération sénégalaise de football (FSF) avait annoncé la réception du Mozambique au stade Léopold Sédar Senghor de Dakar, les Lions devront finalement se déplacer à Maputo pour affronter les Mambas. L’information a été officialisée ce mercredi 9 septembre par la Fédération mozambicaine de football (FMF). Dans un communiqué, l’instance indique que la rencontre se tiendra au Stade national Zimpeto, à Maputo, le 25 septembre à 15 heures, soit à la même date et à la même heure que celles initialement prévues. Une demande de la Fédération sénégalaise Selon la FMF, cette délocalisation fait suite à une demande de la Fédération sénégalaise de football. Le stade Abdoulaye Wade, qui aurait initialement été retenu pour cette rencontre, serait indisponible en raison de la tenue des Jeux olympiques régionaux. Cette situation intervient alors que le site officiel de la Fédération sénégalaise de football annonçait encore le stade Léopold Sédar Senghor comme enceinte devant accueillir la rencontre. La demande sénégalaise aurait été acceptée par le sélectionneur mozambicain Chiquinho Condé, avant de recevoir l’approbation de la Confédération africaine de football (CAF). Les Lions privés de leur public Cette modification constitue un changement important pour les Lions, qui perdent ainsi l’avantage de jouer à domicile. Au lieu de recevoir les Mambas devant leur public, les Lions devront désormais se produire à Maputo, avec les contraintes liées à un déplacement à l’extérieur. Le rendez-vous du 25 septembre reste donc maintenu, mais le décor change radicalement : les Lions devront aller chercher au Mozambique les points nécessaires dans leur course à la qualification pour la CAN 2027. A.N

items.title: Why Trump Has It Out for Canada
items.description: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here. When Donald Trump looks at a map, he doesn’t see nations. He sees property. All of those pretty colors do not represent actual places filled with human beings who have distinct cultures, languages, and histories; the planet, to Trump, is a big board game, like Risk or Monopoly. Greenland isn’t a real location—it’s a valuable chunk of territory nestled between Boardwalk and Park Place. The Strait of Hormuz isn’t an international waterway—it’s a thing to control somewhere between Kamchatka and East Africa. This inability to grasp the existence of independent nations drives the president to fury when countries and their governments refuse to play along with his delusions. Trump cannot understand why Iran won’t bend to his will, why NATO won’t instantly obey his orders, why South Korea and Japan won’t just write checks or provide troops on demand. The only people Trump seems to respect are the autocrats in Beijing and Moscow and Pyongyang who, like him, view the world as a brutal competition for power and territory. Now Trump has declared economic war on Canada, a nation that has vexed him for years. Even by the standards of Trump’s many fixations, his obsession with Canada has become not only weird but truly destructive. He has opened a giant political and economic rift with one of America’s biggest trading partners, a sister nation, and an ally in the common defense of North America and Europe. Why does Trump hate Canada so much? We can only speculate about what goes on in the president’s head, but his actions suggest a pattern. When Trump is frustrated about something he can’t control, he lashes out at friends harder than he does enemies. He took out his anger about the Epstein files on legislators from his own party, even though he had campaigned on releasing those documents. Stymied by Iran on multiple fronts, Trump decided to blame South Korea for not helping him, and curtailed military exercises with a vital U.S. ally. (This decision also had the side benefit of allowing Trump to make another embarrassing overture to the North Korean dictator Kim Jong Un, a bromantic gesture that went unreciprocated.) Trump values absolute loyalty over everything else—not that he always returns it—and he detests any sign that others, especially those who are supposed to be his friends and allies, might have views and interests of their own. The American economy is stalling, and Trump’s poll numbers are in the basement, so the next obvious move is to pick a huge fight with a nation that is essentially family to Americans. Canada is most definitely a foreign country, which is one reason I like to visit. (Go ahead—try to find a convenience store in America that sells Aero chocolate bars or wine gums.) But to the utterly incurious Trump, it probably looks like an extension of upstate New York. Canada and America are bound by deep cultural and historical bonds, but ironically, the superficial similarities are likely driving much of Trump’s vitriol. How dare these people—whose country is, to him, just a cheap knockoff of America—defy him! After all, most of Canada speaks English; its cities look like ours (if definitely cleaner); we share pop stars and TV shows; they even call their money “the dollar,” despite its colorful look and plasticky feel. Canada, in the president’s eyes, is less a sovereign nation than a real-estate parcel he forgot to buy because it’s in a neighborhood he never visits. The fact that Canada is led by someone Trump accidentally helped put in office probably irks him too. Early last year, Canada’s Liberal Party had been in power for 10 years and was facing a huge defeat in what seemed to be an impending “change” election. Trump, as usual, could not control himself when it came to the internal politics of an allied nation: He imposed tariffs during the lead-up to the Canadian vote while banging on about making Canada the 51st state. The Liberal leader Mark Carney—an unflappable public figure who is completely different from Trump in both temperament and intellect—pivoted quickly and campaigned on standing up to the American president. Carney almost overnight went from a no-hoper to prime minister. And now he has shown that he is perfectly willing to retaliate against Trump’s policies rather than fold. If Trump wants tariffs, Carney will provide them—in spades. Imagine how all of this looks to Trump, who has made clear that Canada shouldn’t even exist as an independent state. I am humiliated as an American, and as a friend of Canada, to admit this, but Trump’s attitude toward Canada is almost indistinguishable from the way Russian President Vladimir Putin sees Ukraine: not as a state but as some kind of historical anomaly that should be returned to its rightful owners. Trump might think it’s funny to post memes of Canada with an American flag superimposed on it, but those jokes are a lot less hilarious to people in places such as Ukraine, who are fighting a war against a dictator who feels exactly the same way about their country. Canadians are probably scratching their head over Trump’s willingness to hurt his own people and especially his own party. Trump may hate Canada, but it’s hard to imagine what he thinks he’ll gain by causing economic pain to Americans along the Canadian border, especially in states such as Maine and Michigan, where Republicans are facing tight battles for congressional seats. What the Canadians may not realize is that, with this president, none of it has to make sense, and that if recent history is a guide, he will back down, perhaps after declaring victory over Ottawa. Trump will then move on, leaving ordinary Americans and their Canadian friends to deal with the damage. Related : Trump will make South Korea pay for his Iran humiliation. How to lose a trade war Here are four new stories from The Atlantic : Mothers for sale How 9/11 changed New York—and America Does Trump want Republicans to win the midterms? The inside story of what happened at Stars and Stripes Today’s News Last night, U.S. forces struck five Iranian oil tankers , sinking one, after Iran targeted a U.S. Navy warship. Iran retaliated by firing missiles at an air base in Jordan that the U.S. uses. Jordan said it received 20 ballistic missiles and was able to destroy 18. Republican former Senator John Sununu and Democratic Representative Chris Pappas won their U.S. Senate primaries in New Hampshire last night, setting up a competitive general-election race in November. items.title: Internet par satellite: la Sonatel obtient la suspension provisoire de la licence de Starlink
items.description: La Cour suprême a ordonné lundi 07 septembre la suspension provisoire de la licence accordée à Starlink Sénégal pour fournir des services d’accès à internet fixe par satellite. À l’origine de cette procédure, la Sonatel, qui conteste l’autorisation délivrée à la filiale sénégalaise de Space X. Pour l’opérateur historique, l’ouverture de ce marché doit tenir compte de ses investissements et des obligations auxquelles il est soumis dans le cadre de sa concession. Le contentieux porte sur l’arrêté ministériel n°038974 du 6 novembre 2025, par lequel l’ancien ministre chargé de la Communication, des Télécommunications et du Numérique, Alioune Sall, avait autorisé Starlink Sénégal Suarl à exploiter, pour une durée de cinq ans, un service d’accès à internet fixe par satellite, rapportent plusieurs sites d’informations visités par « Le Soleil ». L’autorisation reposait notamment sur un cahier des charges établi par l’Autorité de régulation des télécommunications et des postes (Artp). Pour contester cette décision, la Sonatel met en avant son statut de titulaire d’une licence individuelle de premier rang, encadrée par les décrets de 2016 et de 2023 portant approbation de sa convention de concession et de ses cahiers des charges. L’entreprise estime que l’arrivée de Starlink dans ces conditions est susceptible de porter atteinte à ses intérêts économiques ainsi qu’aux règles de concurrence et à ses droits de défense. Mardi dernier, lors de la déclaration de politique générale du Premier ministre, le député Mamadou Mory Diaw avait demandé au chef du gouvernement de confirmer la nouvelle de la suspension de la licence de Starlink. Dans sa défense, l’opérateur historique insiste particulièrement sur l’ampleur de ses engagements financiers. Selon les éléments rapportés par le site d’informations, la Sonatel fait état de 100 milliards de francs CFA de droits et redevances, dont 68 milliards liés au renouvellement de sa concession et 32 milliards au titre des fréquences 4G. À cette somme s’ajoutent 34,5 milliards de francs CFA versés pour l’acquisition des licences 5G. Au total, l’entreprise met donc en avant 134,5 milliards de francs CFA engagés au titre de ces droits et licences. La Sonatel souligne également les obligations qui découlent de son statut d’opérateur titulaire d’une licence de premier rang. Celles-ci portent notamment sur la couverture du territoire, le service universel, la continuité et la qualité des services. L’entreprise rappelle aussi les contributions financières auxquelles elle est assujettie, notamment au Fonds de développement du service universel des télécommunications (FDSUT) et au titre des redevances annuelles. La procédure judiciaire engagée par la Sonatel n'est pas intervenue immédiatement après la délivrance de l'autorisation à Starlink. L'opérateur avait d'abord introduit, le 10 mars 2026, un recours gracieux auprès du ministère de tutelle. Cette démarche n'ayant pas mis fin au différend, le dossier a finalement été porté devant la Cour suprême. Selon le site spécialisé en Tic, osiris.sn, « le dossier Starlink a été marqué par plusieurs épisodes de tension avec la régulation sénégalaise. Avant même l’obtention de sa licence, l’entreprise avait fait l’objet, dès 2023, d’une répression de la commercialisation informelle de ses terminaux, l’Autorité de régulation des télécommunications et des postes (ARTP) ayant fait interpeller plusieurs revendeurs non autorisés ». Après l’entrée en service officielle, l’Artp a de nouveau alerté, fin mars 2026, contre la prolifération de points de « wifi communautaire » exploitant des terminaux Starlink pour de la revente illégale de connexion, rappelant que ces pratiques exposent leurs auteurs à des peines pouvant aller jusqu’à cinq ans de prison et 60 millions de francs CFA d’amende. Des interpellations similaires ont encore eu lieu au mois d’août 2026, notamment à Kaolack, à la suite d’une plainte de la Sonatel. De son côté, l'autorisation de Starlink s'inscrivait dans le cadre du « New Deal Technologique », programme gouvernemental destiné notamment à accélérer la couverture numérique du territoire. Le dispositif prévoyait entre autres l'acquisition par l'État de 5 000 kits Starlink à tarif préférentiel, afin de contribuer à la desserte des zones blanches, au déploiement de réseaux wifi communautaires ainsi qu'à la connexion d'établissements scolaires et de collectivités territoriales. items.title: EuroMed Droits appelle à la libération immédiate de Mohamed Yousfi
items.description: EuroMed Droits exprime sa profonde préoccupation à la suite de l’émission d’un mandat de dépôt à l’encontre du journaliste Mohamed Yousfi, rédacteur en chef du site d’information Al Katiba, et appelle à sa libération immédiate. Mohamed Yousfi a été arrêté alors qu’il se rendait dans les locaux de la radio Express FM pour participer à une émission radiophonique, puis placé en garde à vue. Le jour de son arrestation, Mohamed Yousfi avait subi une intervention chirurgicale urgente. Malgré les douleurs importantes dont il souffrait, il a été interrogé et le juge d’instruction a ensuite émis, le mercredi 8 septembre, un mandat de dépôt à son encontre. EuroMed Droits exprime sa profonde inquiétude face à cette affaire, qui s’inscrit dans une tendance croissante de restrictions systématiques visant les voix indépendantes et critiques, notamment les journalistes, les syndicalistes, les responsables politiques, les défenseur·e·s des droits humains et les acteurs de la société civile. Les avocats de la défense ont notamment affirmé que le dossier ne contenait aucun document, aucune preuve, ni même le moindre commencement de preuve justifiant l’émission d’un mandat de dépôt à son encontre. L’affaire de Mohamed Yousfi s’inscrit dans un contexte plus large de ciblage des journalistes tunisiens indépendants. D’autres journalistes sont actuellement détenus ou font l’objet de poursuites judiciaires, notamment Mourad Zeghidi, Borhen Bsaïss et Zied El Héni. EuroMed Droits condamne également le climat d’intimidation, de stigmatisation et de diffamation visant les journalistes et les voix critiques, et souligne que ces pratiques sont contraires à la liberté de la presse et au droit des citoyen·ne·s d’accéder à l’information. EuroMed Droits appelle les autorités tunisiennes à : Libérer immédiatement Mohamed Yousfi et poursuivre l’enquête à son encontre en état de liberté ; Garantir le respect de la présomption d’innocence, des droits de la défense et du droit à un procès équitable ; Mettre fin à l’utilisation abusive du droit pénal contre les journalistes en raison de l’exercice de leur profession et de leur droit à la liberté d’expression ; Garantir un environnement sûr et indépendant permettant aux journalistes d’exercer leur profession sans menaces, intimidations ni poursuites arbitraires. The accident occurred on Monday, September 7, 2026, while the campaign team was travelling from Tumu in the Upper West Region to Wa, after a campaign engagement in Bolgatanga in the Upper East Region. A statement issued by the campaign team, copied to the Ghana News Agency and signed by Alhaji Suwaari Ibrahim A-Rahman, Spokesperson of the campaign team, said persons who sustained injuries in the accident had been treated and discharged, while one person had been transferred to the Wenchi Methodist Hospital for further medical attention. items.title: CDD-Ghana pushes for independent authority to regulate political financing
items.description: The Centre for Democratic Development (CDD-Ghana) is advocating the establishment of an independent authority to regulate political party and campaign financing in Ghana. The Centre says the proposed authority will help address gaps in the existing regulatory framework and curb the growing monetisation of politics in the country. Joseph Oti Frimpong, Programmes Officer at CDD-Ghana, announced this during a media workshop on regulating political party financing in Ghana, organised by the Centre in Kumasi and funded by the British High Commission. He presented CDD-Ghana’s draft model law on political finance and the Government’s position paper on the recommendations of the Constitution Review Commission (CRC) on curbing money in politics. Mr Oti Frimpong said the existing legal framework largely regulated political parties but did not adequately cover candidates and electoral campaign financing. He said the gaps had contributed to challenges, including high campaign costs, unregulated private funding, inadequate disclosure of political financing, vote-buying, and abuse of state resources. The CDD-Ghana draft model law proposes the establishment of an Independent Electoral Financing and Enforcement Authority (IEFEA) to oversee political finance regulation, monitoring, enforcement, audits and disclosure. The proposed Authority would have powers to issue regulations, conduct investigations and audits, subpoena witnesses, impose fines and sanctions and refer cases for prosecution. Under the proposal, all campaign transactions would be conducted through designated campaign bank accounts, which would be subject to periodic and forensic audits. The Authority would also set expenditure limits for party primaries, by-elections, and general elections, taking into account factors such as geography, population, infrastructure, and the type of election. Mr Oti Frimpong said candidates would be required to submit financial reports detailing their campaign receipts and expenditure, with the reports published online to promote public scrutiny. The draft law also proposes limits on contributions, restrictions on anonymous donations above a specified threshold and measures to enhance transparency in third-party spending. Mr Frimpong identified the monetisation of politics, vote-buying, unregulated financing of candidates, and abuse of state resources as some of the major challenges confronting Ghana’s political financing architecture. The Constitution Review Commission has similarly recommended the establishment of an Independent Registrar and Regulator of Political Parties and Campaigns (IRRPC) with powers to register and regulate political parties, impose sanctions, and address issues such as vote-buying. The CRC also proposed restrictions on the campaign period, regulation of campaign receipts and expenditure, external audits of party and candidate funding, and sanctions for abuse of incumbency. The Government, however, has accepted in principle the need for an independent body but prefers a Political Parties Regulatory Commission (PPRC), to be established through ordinary legislation rather than the IRRPC proposed by the CRC. It has also acknowledged the need for campaign finance legislation covering expenditure caps, disclosure thresholds, and enforcement mechanisms. Mr Frimpong said the ongoing discussions presented an opportunity for stakeholders to close the regulatory gaps and establish a political financing system that would promote transparency, accountability and fairness in Ghana’s democratic process.

items.title: Kagbélén : deux personnes tuées après qu’une moto s’est retrouvée sous un camion
items.description: Un accident mortel de la circulation a coûté la vie à deux personnes ce mercredi 9 septembre 2026, à Kagbélén Village-Mosquée. Le drame s’est produit aux environs de 16 heures, sur la route nationale numéro 2 (RN2), à proximité d’une mosquée. Les deux victimes se trouvaient à bord d’une moto qui s’est retrouvée sous un camion. L’accident a attiré plusieurs riverains et usagers de la route, venus constater les faits. Selon les témoignages recueillis sur place, une moto transportant deux personnes, dont une femme, a été impliquée dans un accident avec un camion. Ibrahima Sory Camara, connu sous le surnom de Kassory, chef du secteur de Kagbélén Village-Mosquée, dit avoir assisté à la scène. « Nous étions assis au bord de la route. Un motard arrivait avec une dame assise derrière lui. Au même moment, le camion était devant. Je ne sais pas si le motard voulait rentrer, mais c’est le deuxième pneu du camion qui a rattrapé la moto. Ils sont tombés et ils ont succombé sur place », témoigne-t-il. Aly Badara Traoré, un autre témoin rencontré sur les lieux, livre une autre version des circonstances de l’accident. Selon lui, le conducteur de la moto aurait perdu le contrôle avant de se retrouver sous le camion. « Nous étions arrêtés, nous avons vu le conducteur de la moto venir, le camion partait vers Conakry. Le motard a voulu prendre le frein, mais malheureusement il n’a pas réussi. C’est ainsi que la moto les a tirés sous le camion. Le conducteur du camion ne s’est même pas rendu compte qu’il y avait un danger autour de lui. C’est nous qui avons crié pour l’alerter », explique-t-il. D’après ce témoignage, la moto venait de Grand Moulin en direction de Dubréka et aurait quitté sa trajectoire avant de finir sous le camion. Après le drame, les corps des deux victimes ont été transportés à l’hôpital préfectoral de Dubréka pour les formalités d’usage. items.title: Indonesian Military Court Reduces Acid Attack Sentences
items.description: Click to expand Image Andrie Yunus, deputy coordinator at KontraS, attending a protest in Bandar Lampung, Sumatra on February 5, 2026. © 2026 Project Multatuli/Adrian Mulya A military court in Jakarta reduced the prison sentences and overturned the dishonorable discharge of two of the four military personnel convicted for the March 2026 acid attack against human rights activist Andrie Yunus. The appellate decision, dated August 20, reduced the sentences of 2nd Sgt. Edi Sudarko and 1st Lt. Budhi Hariyanto Widhi Cahyono of the Indonesian military’s Strategic Intelligence Agency (BAIS) by six months, bringing both sentences to less than three years. The appeals court upheld the shorter sentences of the other two defendants, Capt. Nandala Dwi Prasetya and 1st Lt. Sami Lakka. On March 12, Yunus, 27, the deputy coordinator of KontraS, the nongovernmental Commission for the Disappeared and Victims of Violence, had just finished recording a podcast interview at the Indonesian Legal Aid Foundation when he was attacked with acid. He received 24 percent burns to his face, chest, and hands, and may have lost sight in his right eye. On June 10, a military court found all four soldiers guilty of planning and carrying out the attack. Indonesia’s Judicial Commission, an independent constitutional state body that monitors and oversees the conduct of judges, alleged on July 30 that the military panel that initially tried the case had committed unspecified ethical violations. An internal investigation into the alleged violations is ongoing. A military court investigated and tried the four soldiers because, under Indonesian law, civilian police cannot investigate military personnel. These legal restrictions have long prevented civilian prosecutions of members of the armed forces for serious human rights violations. In 2010, Human Rights Watch urged the Indonesian Parliament to enact a bill that would provide civilian court jurisdiction over members of the military for all crimes committed against civilians. Muhammad Afif Abdul Qoyim, a lawyer from the Indonesian Legal Aid Foundation, said the soldiers should have been tried in civilian courts. He told Human Rights Watch that the Constitutional Court should grant the petition in a judicial review that would push “military courts to handle only military discipline, not ordinary crimes.” Indonesian Human Rights Minister Natalius Pigai has criticized the appellate ruling. But the Indonesian government should go further and order an independent, civilian-led investigation into the attack on Andrie Yunus to hold everyone involved, including those who ordered the attack, accountable.

items.title: Scène de crime horrible en Haïti: Une jeune femme hachée et décapitée avec la complicité de sa meilleure amie, la scène filmée
items.description: C'est l'une des vidéos les plus violentes et les plus cruelles que le monde ait jamais connues. D'une sauvagerie indescriptible, cette séquence montrant l'exécution à la machette d'une jeune internaute surnommée « Baby Love » secoue profondément Haïti. À l'origine de ce drame figure une enquête d'amateur sur l'application Snapchat, ayant mis en lumière les liaisons secrètes de l'influenceuse Esther Thomas, alias « Nice B », avec le chef du redoutable gang des 400 Mawozo. Fureur, vengeance et violation de la loi de l'omertà ont conduit au kidnapping puis à l'assassinat de la victime. Face à l'immense vague d'indignation provoquée par la diffusion en ligne de cette mise à mort, le Parquet de la Croix-des-Bouquets et la DCPJ ont lancé, le 5 septembre 2026, un avis de recherche contre l'influenceuse pour assassinat et association de malfaiteurs, illustrant de manière effroyable le climat de terreur qui gangrène le pays depuis 2021. Dans la pénombre d'une scène éclairée par des projecteurs et des lampes de téléphones portables, la sauvagerie a franchi un cap qui dépasse l'entendement. La victime, une jeune internaute connue sous le pseudonyme de « Baby Love », a été soumise à une agression d'une extrême brutalité. Dans une séquence vidéo de quelques minutes largement relayée sur Internet, la jeune femme, étendue au sol, est hachée et découpée vivante à la machette tour à tour par deux hommes et par sa propre amie, la tiktokeuse Esther Thomas, dite « Nice B ». Loin de chercher à se dissimuler, les agresseurs ont délibérément enregistré leur forfait afin de diffuser la vidéo à grande échelle sur les réseaux sociaux. Aux origines du drame : Enquête sur Snapchat, omertà et rage de vengeance https://netafrique.net/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/NetAfrique_Babylove_reportage_45s_paysage.mp4 Les motifs de cet acte d'une cruauté inimaginable trouvent leur racine dans l'univers virtuel. Tout a débuté lorsqu'une jeune internaute particulièrement observatrice a analysé des publications éphémères sur l'application Snapchat. En observant la couleur d'une chambre et la disposition d'un lit concordant entre deux comptes distincts, elle a publié une vidéo affirmant par « A + B » que son amie « Nice B » partageait en secret la vie du chef des 400 Mawozo, l'un des gangs les plus redoutés du pays. La publication insinuait également une complicité active de l'influenceuse au sein du réseau criminel. Saisie d'une rage noire face à ces révélations menaçant sa sécurité, l'influenceuse aurait réclamé « la tête » de l'internaute pour assouvir sa vengeance. La victime a ensuite été traquée, kidnappée puis livrée à ses bourreaux. Traquée par la justice : Le mandat d'arrêt contre Esther Thomas https://netafrique.net/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/fget.io_1788989457632.mp4 Face à l'immense vague d'indignation et à la diffusion de ces images insoutenables, l'appareil judiciaire haïtien est sorti de son silence. Par une réquisition datée du 5 septembre 2026, le Parquet près le Tribunal de première instance de la Croix-des-Bouquets a ordonné la recherche et l’arrestation immédiate d'Esther Thomas. Dans la foulée, la Police Nationale d'Haïti (PNH) et la Direction Centrale de la Police Judiciaire (DCPJ) ont diffusé un avis de recherche national ciblant « Nice B » ainsi que Darlens Duclona, alias « Enspektè tèt kale ». Tous deux sont formellement poursuivis pour des chefs d'accusation d'assassinat, de tentative d'assassinat et d'association de malfaiteurs, scellant la fin de la carrière de créatrice de contenu d'Esther Thomas et le début de sa cavale criminelle. Haïti sous le règne de la terreur : L’emprise des gangs et la propagande par l'image Ce crime odieux met en lumière la crise sécuritaire et humanitaire sans précédent qui ravage Haïti. Depuis l'assassinat du président Jovenel Moïse, survenu le 7 juillet 2021 dans sa résidence lors d'une attaque par un commando armé, l'effondrement des institutions étatiques a accéléré l’emprise des cartels de la mafia et des gangs armés comme les 400 Mawozo, fortement implantés à la Croix-des-Bouquets. Ces groupes criminels ont transformé la violence extrême en outil de propagande, d'intimidation et de domination psychologique en utilisant les réseaux sociaux pour amplifier l'impact de leurs actes. Les chiffres publiés par l'ONU pour les premiers mois de l'année 2026 témoignent de cette tragédie nationale : entre janvier et début juin 2026, au moins 2 310 personnes ont été tuées, 1 106 blessées et 99 enlevées dans le pays, abandonné à la loi de la jungle. L’article Scène de crime horrible en Haïti: Une jeune femme hachée et décapitée avec la complicité de sa meilleure amie, la scène filmée est apparu en premier sur NetAfrique.net .

items.title: New York, 25 Years Later
items.description: Photographs by Sasha Arutyunova L ike most New Englanders of a certain generation, my parents viewed New York City with distrust. They associated their neighbor to the south with “The Bronx Is Burning,” Bernhard Goetz, blackouts, bankruptcy, and the famous New York Daily News headline Ford to City: Drop Dead . The heart of Manhattan was a decadent playground for the wealthy, while outlying neighborhoods were plagued by desperate poverty and violence. I grew up only 200 miles away, and yet my parents never took me there as a kid. But if New York felt menacing and foreign to them, in reality, it is the most American of cities. New York is a symbol of the nation’s money and power, its diversity and freedom. It is our capital of culture, a proudly loud and bustling melting pot. And for those who wanted to humble the world’s sole superpower, New York was the perfect place to strike 25 years ago this week. Two of its signature skyscrapers were toppled, and nearly 3,000 lives were lost. The response underscored how much New York belongs to America. Rescue workers from red and blue states raced to help. Donations poured in from rich California cities and small Montana towns. American flags were seemingly everywhere. For the first time in decades, and less than a year after a bitterly contested presidential election, the nation felt unified. We’ve been chasing that feeling ever since. New York City has bounced back—revitalized and thriving—with a new skyline emerging from the dust. But the nation is deeply divided, with angrier elections and escalating political violence. The pandemic could have brought the sort of unity we felt after the terror attacks, but it instead largely fostered division and rage. There is a new conflict in the Middle East, one whose dubious origins evoke the misguided war launched there after the World Trade Center fell. And now, a quarter century after the September 11 attacks, a New Yorker is president, one who was in Manhattan that crystal-clear, late-summer day. But Donald Trump won’t be there on Friday. M y first visit to New York City included the World Trade Center. I was in high school when, in 1995, my brother and I joined a church-group trip down from Massachusetts (my parents still wanted no part of it) to Liberty and Ellis Islands. I remember the ferry ride back to Lower Manhattan at the day’s end, staring at those impossibly tall towers. I was transfixed. Later, I was lucky enough to go to college in New York, and immersed myself in its energy. The Twin Towers were not exactly beloved architecture, but they were a constant, comforting presence; when you got out of the subway downtown, below the city’s street grid, the easiest way to orient yourself was to locate the World Trade Center. Find those towers, and you could get yourself anywhere. You could get yourself home. Sasha Arutyunova for The Atlantic On September 11, 2001, I was a 21-year-old intern at the New York Daily News and, with no money to my name, was between apartments and sleeping on my friend’s couch. It was Primary Day, and I had the morning off ahead of covering some comptroller candidate’s Election Night party. My friend’s nanny had the television on, and I heard her shriek. Al-Qaeda got what it wanted: As the world watched the first tower burn, the second was hit. I grabbed my notebook and tried to get to work. But I was staying uptown, at West 120th Street, and the subways were already a mess and soon shut completely. I couldn’t reach the newspaper’s assignment desk; the phones were overloaded. So I started walking south, toward the World Trade Center, trying to listen to updates on my portable radio. Not long after the towers fell, I connected with an editor who diverted me to a major hospital with a trauma center, to witness the arrival of the injured. I was instead confronted by a jarring and heartbreaking image: rows of empty hospital beds. The scores of survivors never came; there simply weren’t many. The sky was incongruously beautiful. When the wind turned, I could smell the smoke, an acrid blend of jet fuel and steel and other things too sad to consider. My next stop, after nightfall, was a bereavement center set up farther downtown. I fielded as many questions as I asked and desperate pleas from frantic people—some covered in ash—looking for information about their missing loved ones. Soon, the city would be dotted with homemade signs about those who were lost, posters hung by families clinging to hope. Many would stay up for months. On September 12, I slipped past the security perimeter and reached Ground Zero. I was there, off and on, for days, trying to describe the indescribable to the newspaper’s readers. The rubble continued to burn. Debris and body parts were everywhere. Firefighters refused breaks, as they dug for their fallen brothers. There was a pervasive sense of fear: It seemed as if anything could happen, including more attacks. [ Read: The man who refused to sit on the sidelines ] The four hijacked airplanes had attacked symbols of the United States’ financial might (the World Trade Center), its military (the Pentagon), and its democracy (the U.S. Capitol or the White House were the likely target of a fourth plane that passengers forced to crash in the Pennsylvania countryside). The sense of loss and disruption was overwhelming. Many nights, I cried myself to sleep. It felt as if life would never return to normal; even the small routines—going to an office, riding the subway, going to a baseball game—seemed newly fragile. In the weeks that followed, I covered dozens of funerals. Traditionally, when a New York firefighter dies, much of the department attends. But that terrible fall and winter, many of the city’s firefighters were still working long shifts digging through the pile at Ground Zero. To make sure that each service was robustly attended, hundreds—and, at times, thousands—of firefighters journeyed from departments across the country. The funerals invariably included a version of “Amazing Grace” from the FDNY’s pipes-and-drums band. To this day, I have a hard time hearing bagpipes. Sasha Arutyunova for The Atlantic Y et even in those first hours , there were signs of hope. The city’s mayor, Rudy Giuliani, had woken up that morning as an unpopular lame duck, a self-styled political brawler whose success fighting crime had been overshadowed by his personal foibles and executive overreach. But with President George W. Bush largely out of sight that day, Giuliani became the face of a mourning, yet determined, city. His leadership in the weeks that followed was nothing short of heroic. He was followed into office by Michael Bloomberg, the billionaire businessman who led the city’s recovery and rebuilding (and personally financed much of the National September 11 Memorial & Museum). In bipartisan fashion, Congress passed a victims-compensation fund. Our NATO allies stood by us, invoking the Article 5 mutual-defense clause for the first and, so far, only time in the alliance’s history. Bush spoke out firmly against Islamophobia. The nation even rallied around the Yankees’ run to the World Series that year. (Okay, maybe not everybody rooted for them.) Despite early conversations about whether anyone would ever want to work or live in Lower Manhattan again, businesses came back, and, in a surprise development, more people moved downtown. As for the World Trade Center site itself, there were certainly turf wars, differing visions, false starts and delays, and probably more new office space than really was needed. But it slowly grew again, anchored by the 1,776-foot-high One World Trade Center and the 9/11 memorial and museum. The tree-lined, eight-acre site was transformed into a peaceful park with two reflecting pools where the towers once stood. Those pools are filled by waterfalls and ringed by the names of the victims . Dennis Mojica. James P. O’Brien Jr. Cindy Yan Zhu Guan. The rest of the city came back too. In the decades that followed, apartment prices skyrocketed, and young people transformed neighborhoods deep into Brooklyn and Queens. Crime plummeted, and the NYPD developed a counterterrorism arm. More skyscrapers soared above Manhattan. Broadway boomed. Tourists arrived in record numbers (and, yes, even my parents warmed to the city). There are still challenges, affordable housing and income inequality among them. But the city today is safer and more vibrant than ever. And in a development that would have been unthinkable a quarter century ago, the year’s September 11 remembrance services will include the city’s 34-year-old democratic socialist Muslim mayor . The city’s communal response to the terror attacks was inspirational: People checked on loved ones and strangers; they donated blood; they saluted first responders. The tragedy also provided a template of sorts for the calamities that would lie ahead. Gone were the stereotypes that New Yorkers didn’t care about their neighbors, or would take advantage of disaster to loot or riot. In their place were scenes of regular people banding together to pull through the 2003 blackout, Hurricane Sandy, and the pandemic. During those fear-filled early months of 2020, One World Trade Center’s top would at times be bathed in red, white, and blue. Sasha Arutyunova for The Atlantic T he city today sits in a far more divided nation. That initial feeling of national unity was dealt a series of body blows, including the Iraq War, the financial panic of 2008, and the racist backlash to the election of the first Black president . The country became angrier, more polarized, more red versus blue, more us versus them. Donald Trump seized the moment. Over the past decade, he has widened the nation’s political and cultural fissures, eroded trust of American institutions, governed like he was president only of his supporters—and moved to punish those who didn’t back him. Giuliani, once heralded as “America’s Mayor,” embraced Trump’s lies about the 2020 election, drawing an indictment, disbarments, and a loss in a $148 million defamation lawsuit over his false claims about two Georgia election workers. [ John Avlon: What happened to Rudy Giuliani? ] Trump has never seemed all that moved by his hometown’s darkest day. Mere hours after the towers fell, he spoke to a local television station, saying that a building he owned had suddenly gained in stature. That building, 40 Wall Street, “actually was the second-tallest building in Downtown Manhattan, and it was actually—before the World Trade Center—was the tallest,” he said. (The claim was inaccurate, as well as insensitive.) Trump has attended the annual memorial at Ground Zero a few times, including in 2024, but will not do so again this week. The New York Times reported that the president is instead participating in a Pentagon event because Manhattan organizers would not let him deliver a speech. (By tradition, there are no speeches delivered at Ground Zero, only a solemn reading of the victims’ names.) It would also be easier for Trump to fly out of Washington to attend a golf tournament this weekend at a course he owns in Ireland. The White House denied that Trump had asked to speak. Trump has long been incapable of bringing people together and uninterested in doing so. He frequently indulges in anti-Muslim rhetoric (emphasizing Barack Obama’s middle name, Hussein, and the full name of Michigan’s Democratic Senate candidate, Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed) and once proposed a travel ban for anyone of that faith. His war against Iran has raised fears of another terror attack. The relationship between the president and his hometown is broken; he rarely visits his Midtown penthouse and is greeted with protests when he does. In all three of his presidential campaigns, he lost badly in New York. And though he has seemed charmed by the city’s new mayor, Zohran Mamdani, that did not stop his administration from announcing the results of a deportation surge for the city—dubbed “Operation Rotten Apple”—just days before the solemn Ground Zero commemoration. New York City has been abandoned by its most famous son. But it will push forward, and it won’t be alone. Former presidents from both parties are slated to attend the ceremony on Friday morning. The commemoration itself is meant for the victims’ families, and officials expect a larger-than-usual turnout. But once the event is over, and the temporary ropes come down, the memorial will again open to the public. I took my sons there earlier this week. We saw people from red states and blue ones, and heard languages from all over the world. Those visitors stared at the waterfalls, let their hands run over the names of those lost, and shared quiet hugs. That will happen again this September 11. And when night falls, the Tribute in Light will switch on and beam pillars of light upward. The illuminated towers will stretch to the heavens—and they’ll guide so many of us home.

items.title: Transport : la contestation s’étend aux professionnels des taxis
items.description: Après que les professionnels du transport routier de marchandises ont annoncé une grève à partir du 14 septembre, en réponse à des difficultés fiscales financières et réglementaires des entreprises des dossiers ainsi que des revendications qu'ils jugent restés sans réponse, c'est au tour des professionnels des taxis de se faire entendre. Alors que les routiers ont annoncé une grève générale dès la semaine prochaine sur fonds d'un dossier revendicatif comprenant plusieurs préoccupations, dont le coût du carburant, en estimant que le soutien accordé au gazole ne permet pas de compenser suffisamment le poids des coûts d’exploitation (une aide estimée à 0,50 dirham par litre) les professionnels des taxis en ville ont dénoncé la baisse des aides gouvernementales sans que cela ne soit annoncé. Dans un communiqué, les professionnels des taxis on dénoncé ce qu'ils décrivent que « la décision surprise du gouvernement de réduire de 40 % la valeur de l’aide destinée aux professionnels du transport routier, concernant la deuxième moitié du mois de juillet, sans avertissement préalable » . « La réduction soudaine de cette aide, sans concertation ni notification préalable, constitue donc un mépris des intérêts de milliers de professionnels et de leurs familles et tire la sonnette d’alarme » , affirment-ils. Les conducteurs de taxis ont appelé le gouvernement à revenir sur cette décision qui n'aurait pas été annoncée lors de l’ouverture des formulaires de demande d’aide, lancée le 6 août 2026 et concernant la période allant du 16 au 31 juillet 2026. « Cette situation soulève de nombreuses interrogations sur la manière dont ce dossier est géré, notamment dans un contexte marqué par la persistance de la hausse des prix des carburants et l’absence de toute justification à cette réduction soudaine » , a écrit la coordination syndicale des professionnels du transport routier. Les prix des carburants au Maroc, poursuit le document, « restent en effet à des niveaux très élevés par rapport à l’évolution des cours du pétrole à l’échelle internationale » et de relever que l’aide exceptionnelle décidée par le gouvernement « n’était ni une faveur ni un privilège accordé aux professionnels ». Le syndicat ajoute que cette aide constituait une réponse directe aux dommages subis par les professionnels du transport en raison de la hausse importante et continue des prix des carburants. Il réclame ainsi le rétablissement du montant initial de l’aide, le paiement des arriérés, ainsi que davantage de transparence sur les critères ayant conduit à sa réduction. Dans son communiqué, la coordination appelle « l’ensemble des organisations syndicales et professionnelles du transport routier au Maroc à unifier leurs rangs et à adopter une position commune afin de défendre les droits et les intérêts des professionnels » . Elle les invite à agir rapidement et de manière responsable face à cette évolution jugée « dangereuse » , tout en privilégiant l’unité et en faisant pression sur le gouvernement pour qu’il corrige cette situation. Cette prise de position des professionnels des taxis intervient alors que le secteur du transport routier de marchandises s’apprête à entamer une grève. La convergence des revendications autour de la question du soutien public et du coût des carburants pourrait ainsi accentuer la pression sur le gouvernement. The post Transport : la contestation s’étend aux professionnels des taxis appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Ghana music industry needs collective public-private investment – UK High Commissioner
items.description: UK High Commissioner to Ghana, Sabah Zita Benson, has called for stronger collaboration between the government and private sector to invest in Ghana’s creative industry, particularly music, arts and tourism. According to her, developing the creative sector should not be the sole responsibility of the government, stressing the need for private-sector investment to complement government efforts. She made the remarks in an interview with JoyNews on the sidelines of a music event in Manchester in the United Kingdom, which featured performances from Ghanaian artistes including Kofi Kinaata, Wendy Shay and Akwaboah. Speaking on the importance of promoting Ghana’s music industry internationally, Ms. Benson said music plays a significant role in telling Ghana’s story and projecting the country onto the global stage. “Music tells a story about a people. And music puts us on the international map. So for me, promoting our music goes a long way, working in the UK and hearing a Kofi Kinaata and Wendy Shays song. It gives me a sense of pride. “People want to know who sang the song, where they’re coming from and they want to visit. So it’s not just about promoting the songs, but it’s also a way of driving tourism, where our culture is being heavily promoted.” She further stressed the importance of investment in the sector, noting that recent government funding for tourism demonstrates the importance attached to the sector. “I think I recently heard that there have been some funds released to the tourism sector that should tell you how important the sector is to the government. But you should also know the promotion and support for the tourism and arts industry should not be one person’s job alone. “It must be collective, the government will do its part and the private sector must also be able to invest in the creative sector. For instance, the private sector can build a film studio where our actors can access it – has to be a private and public partnership.” Ms Benson’s comments highlight the need for a broader approach to developing Ghana’s creative economy, with government providing support while businesses and other private investors contribute infrastructure, funding and other resources. She believes such collaboration could create more opportunities for creatives while strengthening Ghana’s position as a destination for culture, entertainment and tourism. Her comments also reinforce the growing recognition of music and the wider creative industry as important tools for promoting Ghana internationally and attracting visitors interested in the country’s culture and entertainment.

items.title: Jeux de l’AES | Tir à l’arc traditionnel : Le Burkina s’adjuge trois médailles d’or
items.description: La deuxième édition des Jeux de l’Alliance des États du Sahel (AES) se poursuit à Ouagadougou. Ce mercredi 9 septembre 2026, les épreuves de tir à l’arc traditionnel ont eu lieu sur le terrain annexe du Stade du 4-Août. Au terme des confrontations, les archers burkinabè se sont illustrés aussi bien en individuel que par équipes, décrochant trois médailles d’or. Lancés lundi dernier dans la capitale burkinabè, ces jeux réunissent le Burkina Faso, le Mali et le Niger autour de plusieurs disciplines sportives. Le podium avec 2 Burkinabè et un Nigérien Chez les hommes, les tirs se sont effectués à une distance de 25 mètres, contre 15 mètres pour les femmes. Les épreuves se sont disputées en plusieurs séries de six puis de trois flèches. Chez les dames, les archères burkinabè, maliennes et nigériennes se sont affrontées. À l’issue des épreuves individuelles, la Burkinabè Yeri Jeannette Kambou a pris la première place, devançant la Malienne Ramatoulaye Traoré et sa compatriote Kabako Kam. En individuel hommes, le Burkinabè Kopounè Hein s’est également distingué en remportant la première place avec 36 points. Son compatriote Kopotin Ollo termine deuxième, tandis qu’un archer nigérien complète le podium. Épreuve du tir à l'arc La domination burkinabè s’est confirmée par équipes. Chez les femmes, le Burkina Faso l’emporte devant le Niger et le Mali. En compétition mixte, l’équipe burkinabè s’impose à nouveau, suivie du Niger puis du Mali. Lors des confrontations directes, les archers burkinabè ont d’abord disputé des demi-finales face à des représentants nigériens avant les matchs de classement. Ils ont notamment décroché une troisième place dans l’une de ces épreuves. Au total, avec les titres en individuel dames, individuel hommes, par équipe féminine et en mixte, le Burkina Faso signe une prestation remarquée dans le tir à l’arc traditionnel. À l’issue de la compétition, les archers burkinabè repartent avec trois médailles d’or, une enveloppe financière et le trophée mis en jeu. Pour Kopounè Hein, cette victoire est avant tout le fruit du travail. « Il n’y a rien de magique là-dedans. Ce sont les entraînements qui paient. Je n’en suis pas à ma première médaille : j’ai participé à la Semaine nationale de la culture (SNC) et à d’autres compétitions sous-régionales où j’ai déjà été récompensé », a-t-il confié. L'objectif Le champion burkinabè a également encouragé ses adversaires à redoubler d’efforts. « J’encourage mes frères du Niger et du Mali à mieux s’entraîner, car, de ce que j’ai vu, leur niveau de jeu était encore insuffisant », a-t-il ajouté. Rappelons que le lancement officiel des Jeux de l’AES a eu lieu hier au Palais des sports de Ouaga 2000. Les épreuves de tir à l’arc olympique se poursuivront demain, jeudi 10 septembre, sur le même site. Lire aussi : Jeux de l’AES : Les Étalons U17 A écrasent le Niger et lancent parfaitement la compétition Nadège KINDA Minute.bf

items.title: Ligue des champions: le PSG cartonne d'entrée
items.description: Le Paris Saint-Germain, double champion d'Europe en titre, et le FC Barcelone, en quête d'un sixième titre européen, n'ont pas fait de détails pour leur entrée en lice de Ligue des champions mercredi en s'imposant largement respectivement contre Bratislava (6-1) et le Feyenoord Rotterdam (5-1). Dans les deux affiches du jour, Liverpool a péniblement battu l'Atlético Madrid (2-1) à Anfield, mais perdu Bradley Barcola sur blessure, et Arsenal, finaliste l'an passé, a fini par percer le mur dressé par le Napoli en Italie (1-0), grâce à son capitaine norvégien Martin Odegaard. Le champion rassure. Grâce à son Ballon d'Or Ousmane Dembélé et son champion du monde espagnol Ferran Torres, le PSG, qui n'a pas encore gagné en Ligue 1 après trois journées, a parfaitement lancé sa difficile quête d'un troisième trophée européen consécutif en éparpillant façon puzzle le Slovan Bratislava de Yaya Touré. Dembélé, titulaire dans une équipe remaniée, s'est offert un doublé (17e, 23e), avant de servir deux fois Ferran Torres (31e, 47e), l'attaquant espagnol inscrivant même un triplé (57e), avant que son compatriote et ami Fabian Ruiz n'enfonce un peu plus le clou en fin de rencontre (6-1, 88e). L'adversité devrait être tout autre à l'Etihad Stadium face à Manchester City, le 14 octobre pour la deuxième journée, mais Paris a enfin lancé sa saison avec ce large succès. Liverpool également après des débuts pénibles en Premier League et qui, mené par l'Atléti après un but de Marcos Llorente, est revenu au score grâce à Dominik Szoboszlai (40e), puis s'est imposé sur une frappe de son capitaine argentin Alexis Mac Allister (50e). – Un Barça de feu – Petit bémol pour les Reds, leur ailier français Bradley Barcola est sorti pour une blesure sans gravité, sous les applaudissements du public, à quelques jours de la première annonce de liste de Zinédine Zidane, le nouveau sélectionneur de l'équipe de France, qui présentera son groupe le 18 septembre. Arsenal, l'un des favoris cete saison, a dominé un Napoli timide et maladroit. Il a fallu attendre la 75e minute pour que les Gunners prennent un avantage définitif grâce à Martin Odegaard. Plus tôt dans la soirée, un FC Barcelone beaucoup trop fort a fait exploser le Feyenoord Rotterdam (5-1) au Camp Nou, grâce à un nouveau doublé de son capitaine Raphinha, au génie de Lamine Yamal – un but et deux passes décisives – et à ses deux recrues estivales, Karim Adeyemi et Gabriel Jesus. C'est un tarif qui devient presque habituel, et même la forte pluie qui s’est abattue sur la Catalogne n’a pas empêché le Barça, double champion d’Espagne en titre et en quête d'une sixième Ligue des champions, de poursuivre son début de saison parfait avec une cinquième victoire en cinq rencontres, la quatrième avec cinq buts marqués. Dans les deux derniers matches du jour, un triplé du Bosnien Ermedin Demirović a permis à Stuttgart de disposer facilement des Norvégiens de Stavanger (3-1) et le Sporting Portugal s'est défait de Galatasaray sur le même score. Jeudi, Lens retrouve la C1 après trois ans d'absence au Slavia Prague, et le Bayern Munich, autre prétendant à la victoire finale en juin à Madrid, lance sa campagne à domicile face à Bodoe/Glimt, équipe surprise l'an passé. items.title: Mac Allister scores winner as Liverpool beat Atletico Madrid 2-1
items.description: Alexis Mac Allister did his case for an improved Liverpool contract no harm with the winner as Andoni Iraola got off to a winning Champions League start by beating Atletico Madrid 2-1 on Wednesday. Mac Allister expressed his frustration at not being offered a new deal on the eve of the match, but responded by blasting home from the edge of the box to cap Liverpool’s comeback. Marcos Llorente had given Atletico an early lead before Dominik Szoboszlai levelled before half-time. Victory came at a cost for the Reds, though, as new signing Bradley Barcola limped off with a calf injury. For the first time three players who cost in excess of £100 million ($135 million) were named in the same side as Barcola made his Anfield debut alongside Alexander Isak and Florian Wirtz in the Liverpool attack. Isak fired just wide after a purposeful break by Szoboszlai in an energetic start by Liverpool in the first Champions League game of Iraola’s career. But in their desperation to pour forward, the Reds left themselves wide open to the counter-attack. Atletico were humbled 3-0 by Athletic Bilbao on Saturday to cap an underwhelming start to the season by Diego Simeone’s men. Julian Alvarez’s future has cast a cloud over Atletico on and off the field for the past few months after his desire for a move to Barcelona was steadfastly rejected by the club’s hierarchy. The Argentine was handed his first start of the season and cut open the Liverpool defence for the opening goal. Llorente, who named his dog Anfield after scoring twice in Atletico’s last 16 win over Liverpool in 2020, raced onto Alvarez’s pass to score his fifth goal in three visits to Anfield with the Spanish side. – Barcola’s first start – Only a brilliant save by Alisson Becker denied Alvarez from long range before the Liverpool fightback began. Barcola twice should have marked his first chance to impress his new fanbase with a goal. The French winger, who could cost up to £123 million, failed to squeeze the ball past Jan Oblak with just the giant Slovenian to beat. However, Liverpool kept the attack alive and Ronald Araujo’s flick teed up Szoboszlai to find the bottom corner on 40 minutes. Barcola missed an even better chance for his first Liverpool goal when he fired wide after being played in by Wirtz early in the second half. Again, though, the reprieve was brief for the visitors. Mac Allister had been linked with a move to Atletico during the transfer window and expressed his sadness at not being offered a new contract by Liverpool, while Szoboszlai and Ryan Gravenberch have agreed new deals in recent months. The Argentine international arrowed in a shot from outside the box on his weaker left foot and celebrated wildly in front of the Kop. Liverpool’s joy was short-lived as Barcola pulled up holding his calf before the hour mark in what Iraola will hope is not a serious setback. Iraola will be much happier with his side’s defensive display in the second half. Alvarez fired too close to Alisson with one of the visitors’ few clear sights of goal. A last-ditch challenge by Robin Le Normand denied Isak a third goal to round off a fine night for Liverpool. But Iraola was able to celebrate his first statement win since taking charge. “We don’t have the mindset of sabotage” – NPP on MMDCE election proposal
items.description: The New Patriotic Party (NPP) says it will critically assess the government’s proposed changes to the process for selecting Metropolitan, Municipal and District Chief Executives (MMDCEs), with a view to supporting measures that strengthen Ghana’s decentralisation system. The NPP Deputy General Secretary, Haruna Mohammed, said the party would not approach the proposal with a mindset of political sabotage, despite accusing the National Democratic Congress (NDC) of deliberately frustrating former President Nana Akufo-Addo’s attempt to introduce the election of MMDCEs. Speaking on JoyFM’s Top Story on Wednesday, September 9, he recalled the controversy surrounding former President Akufo-Addo’s proposal to amend the Constitution to allow MMDCEs to be elected on a partisan basis. According to him, the current Education Minister, Haruna Iddrisu, had previously acknowledged that the proposal was deliberately sabotaged by the NDC when it was presented to Parliament. “You heard what the current Education Minister said when His Excellency Akufo-Addo sent it to Parliament, that they intentionally sabotaged the system. This was on tape,” he said. He accused the NDC of frustrating the proposal despite knowing that it could have benefited Ghana’s decentralisation system. He, however, said the NPP would not adopt the same approach to the current proposal. “But we as NPP, we don’t think that way. We don’t have that mindset of sabotage, and we’ll look at it with a critical eye, something that is going to help our decentralisation system,” he said. Mr Mohammed also questioned whether the government’s proposed arrangement would significantly change the existing system for appointing MMDCEs. He argued that although the proposed process may increase the number of people involved in voting, the President would still retain significant influence over who becomes an MMDCE. “The only difference between them is the number of people voting for them, but there is nothing that has changed in terms of who is appointing them,” he said. He explained that under the proposed arrangement, five candidates would first be appointed before undergoing a public service interview. “Going through a public service interview doesn’t change anything. It’s just the mode in which the people have been interviewed,” he said. According to him, the President already appoints MMDCEs in consultation with other stakeholders, as provided for under the Constitution. “So if you are saying that the President appoints five and then they go, it’s the same thing. Who appoints them? It’s the same President,” he argued. He said the major difference would be the number of people involved in choosing the final candidate. “That is the difference. Other than that, it’s still the same thing,” he added. The NPP Deputy General Secretary called for a broader and dispassionate national discussion on the proposed reforms, saying the issue should not be reduced to partisan politics. “We should be genuine to make sure that we reflect what we say, and that is what the NDC lacks. What they say is completely different from what they do,” he said. He also urged stakeholders, including organised labour, to continue contributing to discussions on the proposed reforms. “I believe that let’s have a dispassionate discussion around some of these things because it affects everybody. It doesn’t only affect the political systems,” he said. According to him, ordinary citizens are ultimately the beneficiaries of Ghana’s governance system and should therefore remain at the centre of discussions about political and constitutional reforms. “The final consumer of the governance system is a citizen of Ghana, which must be a source of worry for all of us,” he said. He maintained that the NPP would assess the proposal based on whether it ultimately benefits citizens and strengthens Ghana’s decentralisation system.

items.title: From Kumasi to the world: Mirakilouz Beatz’s rise in music production
items.description: Ghanaian music producer Agyei Mensah Miracle, professionally known as Mirakilouz Beatz, is carving out a growing presence in Ghana’s music industry while pursuing ambitions that extend beyond music production. Based in Kumasi, the producer has spent nearly a decade developing his craft, working across different sounds and collaborating with artistes from Ghana and other parts of Africa. His production credits include work associated with artistes such as Kuami Eugene, Wendy Shay, King Paluta, Lasmid, Kweku DMC, O’Kenneth, Cubana Chief Priest and Spyki, adding to a growing portfolio as he continues to establish himself within the industry. For Mirakilouz Beatz, however, producing music represents only one aspect of his involvement in the business. He also works as an A&R at Tieme Music Distribution, where his responsibilities include identifying emerging talent, supporting artistes and helping independent musicians navigate the opportunities and challenges of the modern music industry. The role has broadened his perspective beyond the studio, giving him an opportunity to contribute to artist development and the wider music business. As African music continues to attract audiences and industry investment globally, Mirakilouz Beatz is also looking beyond individual production credits. He is working towards building a major African music production brand while exploring digital platforms that could create additional opportunities for artistes and music professionals. Mentorship is another area of interest for the producer, who hopes to support and develop younger music producers entering the industry. His career reflects a changing landscape within Ghana’s music business, where producers are increasingly expanding their roles beyond creating records to become talent developers, entrepreneurs and music executives. With close to a decade of experience and an expanding body of work, Mirakilouz Beatz is positioning himself for a broader role in Ghana’s creative economy, while continuing to build from his roots in Kumasi toward opportunities across Africa and the global music market.

items.title: Low pay making it harder for universities to attract PhD holders – UTAG-UG
items.description: The University of Ghana chapter of the University Teachers Association of Ghana (UTAG-UG) has warned that poor remuneration is making it increasingly difficult for Ghanaian universities to attract highly qualified academics, particularly professionals with PhDs and specialised industry experience. UTAG-UG President, Dr Jerry Joe Harrison, said improving the conditions of service for lecturers and strengthening universities’ capacity to train their own academics would provide a more sustainable solution to faculty shortages than allowing the Ghana Tertiary Education Commission (GTEC) to take over recruitment. Speaking on Accra-based Citi News, Dr Harrison said the remuneration offered to university lecturers was making academic careers unattractive to professionals in specialised and lucrative fields. “If you are being paid, you know, the kind of money that lecturers are being paid, which lawyer would want to leave their law practice, go pursue a PhD, and then come back to the classroom and come and teach?” he asked on Wednesday, September 9. He said the challenge extended beyond the legal profession to other disciplines, including medicine, where professional and practical experience is an important component of academic expertise. Dr Harrison said while universities must maintain high standards in recruiting faculty, rigid academic requirements could make it difficult to fill vacancies in specialised disciplines where PhD holders are limited. He argued that professional experience should also be recognised, particularly in fields where practitioners may be reluctant to abandon established and better-paying careers for academia. His comments come amid UTAG-UG’s ongoing criticism of GTEC over its decision to advertise faculty positions for various public higher education institutions. UTAG has maintained that the recruitment of academic staff should remain the responsibility of individual universities and their established academic and governance structures. Dr Harrison said if GTEC is concerned about universities struggling to recruit qualified academics, it should support institutions to develop the capacity to produce more PhD holders in areas where expertise is scarce. “As an advisor, if an institution is having difficulty recruiting, you could easily help the institution to set up a PhD programme, through which they can channel people who can then come back and help the institution,” he said. According to him, such an approach would provide a longer-term solution by allowing universities to train academics in specialised areas and build a pipeline of qualified faculty. He added that universities already assess national development needs when determining their research and training priorities and could similarly identify areas where additional academic capacity is required. “Nothing is wrong with that,” Dr Harrison said, arguing that institutions facing shortages in particular disciplines could be supported to develop programmes that produce the expertise needed by universities and the wider economy. He maintained that GTEC should concentrate on its regulatory and advisory mandate rather than assuming responsibility for recruiting academic staff. “We must be guided by the requirements, we must be guided by the availability, we must be guided by the quality of the people that we are receiving,” he said.
