items.title: Pandémies : le Sénégal mobilise 13,89 milliards de francs CFA pour renforcer sa riposte
items.description: Le Sénégal renforce son dispositif de prévention et de réponse aux pandémies. Le ministre de la Santé et de l’Hygiène publique, Ibrahima Sy, a lancé, ce mercredi 09 septembre 2026, un projet triennal d’un montant global de 24,6 millions de dollars soit 13,89 milliards de francs CFA destiné à renforcer les capacités nationales de prévention, de préparation et de riposte face aux futures urgences sanitaires. Face à la multiplication des menaces sanitaires, le pays veut consolider son dispositif de prévention et de riposte. Il vient de lancer le projet « Renforcement des capacités de prévention, de préparation et de riposte aux pandémies », financé par le Pandemic Fund, pour une durée de trois ans. D’un montant global d’environ 24,6 millions de dollars, le programme repose sur l’approche « One Health » ou « Une seule santé ». Celle-ci vise à renforcer la coordination entre les secteurs de la santé humaine, de la santé animale et de l’environnement, considérés comme étroitement liés dans la prévention et la gestion des crises sanitaires. Pour le ministre de la Santé et de l’Hygiène publique, Ibrahima Sy, cette initiative doit permettre au Sénégal de mieux faire face aux risques sanitaires présents et futurs. « Dans un monde où les crises sanitaires sont de plus en plus fréquentes, complexes et interconnectées, cette initiative marque un tournant décisif. Notre ambition est claire : bâtir un système de santé hautement résilient et plus préparé aux risques sanitaires présents et futurs », a-t-il déclaré. Surveillance, laboratoires et ressources humaines Le projet entend notamment renforcer la surveillance épidémiologique et les systèmes d’alerte précoce, les capacités des laboratoires ainsi que les ressources humaines. Trois axes considérés comme prioritaires pour améliorer la préparation du pays face aux éventuelles crises sanitaires. Ces objectifs doivent également permettre au Sénégal de progresser vers un niveau d’excellence en matière de surveillance, de diagnostic et de développement du capital humain, conformément aux exigences du Règlement sanitaire international. « C’est tout le sens du projet que nous consacrons aujourd’hui. Ce projet du Pandemic Fund va permettre de mettre en marche concrètement l’approche de la santé dans toutes les politiques et accélérer la réalisation de la couverture sanitaire universelle », a souligné Ibrahima Sy. Une approche multisectorielle Sous la coordination du ministère de la Santé et de l’Hygiène publique, le projet bénéficie de l’appui technique de plusieurs partenaires, dont la Banque mondiale, l’Organisation mondiale de la santé (OMS), la FAO et l’UNICEF. La coordinatrice sous-régionale de la FAO pour l’Afrique de l’Ouest, Bintia Stephen-Tchicaya, a insisté sur la nécessité d’une mobilisation collective pour assurer la réussite du programme. « Ce lancement n’est pas une fin en soi, mais c’est le point de départ d’une mise en œuvre exigeante qui nécessitera la mobilisation continue de tous : les autorités nationales, les partenaires techniques et financiers, les chercheurs, les communautés à la base et les sociétés civiles », a-t-elle indiqué. Elle estime que la réussite du projet dépendra notamment de la capacité des différents acteurs à dépasser les cloisonnements entre secteurs. De son côté, le représentant de l’UNICEF au Sénégal, Jacques Boyer, a réaffirmé l’engagement de son organisation aux côtés de l’État. « Au nom de l’UNICEF, je réaffirme notre soutien indéfectible aux côtés de l’État du Sénégal, dans un esprit de partenariat transparent et rigoureux, pour que chaque investissement consenti produise un impact durable au bénéfice des populations », a-t-il déclaré. À travers ce financement, le Sénégal entend ainsi consolider les acquis de son système de sécurité sanitaire et mieux anticiper les futures urgences. Les résultats du projet devront être capitalisés, partagés et réutilisés dans l’élaboration des politiques nationales de sécurité sanitaire. A.N

items.title: Apple debuts passport-shaped foldable phone, called Duo
items.description: Apple on Wednesday unveiled a foldable phone called Duo, introducing the biggest change in years in the company’s flagship product. The Duo is sized and shaped like a passport, with rounded edges. It opens into a horizontal, wide screen that can also be viewed vertically. There is a smaller single screen on the front when the phone is folded. When open, it is Apple’s thinnest phone, the company said. The folding phone event, the first with new Chief Executive Officer John Ternus at the helm, is the most noticeable overhaul of Apple’s flagship product since it removed the physical home button from the iPhone X in 2017. The iPhone brought in $209.6 billion, or just over half of Apple’s sales, in its most recent fiscal year. Former CEO Tim Cook handed over the leadership baton to Ternus with a video about how to start the presentation that ended with a close-up of Cook, who said, “Not me. That’s your guy,” pointing back toward Ternus. Ternus touted the iPhone as a personal AI hub that focused on privacy, saying that others wanted to collect and store personal data. “Honestly, trust only goes so far when your data is no longer yours to control,” he said. “That’s why Apple Intelligence runs on device whenever it can.” People look at the new foldable iPhone Duo devices on display during Apple’s event at the Steve Jobs Theater in Cupertino, California, the US on September 9, 2026. — Reuters Apple’s Lilian Rincon, who oversees AI products for the iPhone maker and was recruited from Google earlier this year, described an updated Siri assistant that will work with 300,000 apps at release. Executives also showed off the iPhone 18 Pro and the 18 Pro Max handsets that are the latest versions of Apple’s well-known line, which do not fold. Pricing for the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max starts at $1,199 and $1,299, up $100 from the starting prices of the 17 Pro and Pro Max. Apple also unveiled a feature aimed at addressing growing concerns over AI-generated and manipulated images. It introduced a new standard it calls “Apple Reference Image” to prove the authenticity of the images taken with the new iPhone 18 Pro cameras and said it will also support the emerging SynthID standard for identifying images that have been created or edited with AI. The Apple Reference Image feature will not be available in the EU or China. The iPhone 18 Pro will also include the new A20 Pro chip, which brings improvements to help advanced AI models to run directly on iPhones. Apple CEO John Ternus speaks as Apple holds an event at the Steve Jobs Theater on its campus in Cupertino, California, the US on September 9, 2026. — Reuters “Apple Intelligence and Siri are front and centre. Apple is using its biggest strength, the sheer scale of its hardware base, to make AI an integral part of the everyday experience across devices,” PP Foresight analyst Paolo Pescatore said. Shares were down about one per cent during the Apple presentation. The company also said a new version of AirPods would start at $129 with noise cancellation, a first for its budget line of earbuds, and that a $149 version will be available with extra features such as wireless charging and on-stem volume control that will allow users to adjust the volume by swiping up or down on the stem. Apple also introduced the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4, positioning them as major health-focused upgrades. That includes a redesigned sensor system that collects heart rate more frequently than before and powers new features that gauge recovery and fitness. The company said the watches use new Apple silicon and improved sensors to deliver what it called the most accurate heart-rate tracking in a wearable. Premium pricing challenge Ternus previously served as Apple’s hardware chief but has kept a low public profile aside from a handful of product introductions and sustainability initiatives. It will fall to Ternus to persuade Apple’s customers that they need a foldable device that analysts believe could cost more than $2,000, a new high for a global brand that has defined mass luxury. While Samsung Electronics and Huawei Technologies have sold folding phones since 2019, the devices have remained a niche among tech enthusiasts. But even with a steep price tag, analyst firms such as International Data Corporation expect Apple to sell every foldable iPhone it can produce and secure a 40pc share of the lucrative niche by the end of next year. Wednesday’s event is also expected to mark a major change in Apple’s annual product schedule. While analysts expect Apple to show off new watches, they anticipate the company will hold off on updates to its more affordable iPhone models until next spring and instead focus only on the new folding device and its iPhone Pro and Pro Max lineup. The move is aimed at smoothing out Apple’s annual sales cycle, which typically shows a large bump in revenue during the year-end holiday quarter for the US and Europe.

items.title: Le RNI désigne Salma Benaziz comme porte-parole du parti pendant la campagne électorale
items.description: Le Rassemblement national des indépendants (RNI) a annoncé la désignation de Salma Benaziz en qualité de porte-parole officielle du parti durant la campagne électorale, dans le cadre du renforcement de son dispositif de communication institutionnelle et de l’accompagnement des différentes étapes de la campagne et des prochaines échéances électorales. À ce titre, Salma Benaziz sera chargée de la communication officielle du parti avec les médias nationaux et internationaux. Elle aura également pour mission de présenter les positions du RNI, d’expliquer les grandes lignes de son programme électoral et d’interagir avec les questions et sujets liés à la campagne et à son actualité. Cette nomination intervient dans le cadre de la volonté du RNI de mettre en place une communication claire, organisée et responsable avec l’opinion publique, tout en veillant à ce que les positions, engagements et programme du parti soient transmis aux citoyennes et aux citoyens avec précision et transparence. Le parti estime que cette démarche doit contribuer à rehausser le niveau du débat politique et électoral. Le RNI réaffirme, à cette occasion, son ouverture à l’ensemble des médias et sa disposition à interagir avec eux, ainsi qu’à leur fournir les données et éclaircissements relatifs à ses positions, son programme et ses activités durant les différentes phases de la campagne électorale. The post Le RNI désigne Salma Benaziz comme porte-parole du parti pendant la campagne électorale appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Winners of Ocean Photographer of the Year 2026
items.description: © Jenny Stock / Ocean Photographer of the Year Winner, Female Fifty Fathoms Award. An American crocodile moves through the mangroves of Cuba, a habitat that provides shelter for crocodiles feeding, breeding, nesting, and raising their young. © Marc Lenfant / Ocean Photographer of the Year Finalist, Adventure. Three surfers converge on the same wave at Teahupoʻo, French Polynesia, after a paddler is thrown from his board. The tow-in surfer immediately changes course, grabbing the cameraman to avoid a collision. © Julien Anton / Ocean Photographer of the Year Overall Winner, Ocean Photographer of the Year 2026. An adult seahorse pictured with newly born juveniles in the shallow seaweed-filled waters of Moorea, French Polynesia. While it is not known whether these seahorses are related, their arrangement creates the impression of a farewell, as if the tiny seahorses have gathered around their father after he has released them into the world. © Ajiex Dharma / Ocean Photographer of the Year Finalist, Fine Art. A hinge-back cleaning shrimp rests against a pink barrel sponge in Bali, Indonesia; its eyes are sharply focused while the surrounding colors dissolve into a soft blur. © Jenny Stock / Ocean Photographer of the Year Winner, Female Fifty Fathoms Award. A mother humpback whale and her calf glide through Tonga’s warm, sheltered waters. The calf stays close to its mother at first, then becomes curious, swimming in playful circles and approaching the camera. The mother remains calm and watchful, guiding her young when it comes too close. © Romain Barats / Ocean Photographer of the Year Finalist, Conservation Impact. Three gentoo penguins stand beside the rusting remains of the former Hektor whaling station at Whalers Bay, Deception Island, Antarctica. Once a center for Antarctic whaling, the site is now being reclaimed by wildlife and the harsh polar environment. © Lars von Ritter Zahony / Ocean Photographer of the Year Finalist, Adventure. Sunlight pours through cracks in an iceberg in East Greenland, illuminating the seabed like a natural theater. Created by a storm just days earlier, these openings allow light to reach an underwater world usually hidden in darkness. © Allan Cronin / Ocean Photographer of the Year Finalist, Wildlife. A New Zealand fur seal tears apart a rough skate in the waters of New Zealand, while seabirds gather for the scraps. Unable to swallow such large prey whole, the seal throws the skate repeatedly to break it into smaller pieces. © James Ferrara / Ocean Photographer of the Year Second Place, Fine Art. A common octopus reveals its intricate suckers, textured skin, and watchful eye in the waters of Blue Heron Bridge, Florida. Known for its rich marine life, this shallow dive site provided the setting for a close encounter with one of the ocean’s most intelligent animals. © Richard Condlyffe / Ocean Photographer of the Year Finalist, Fine Art. A ladybug amphipod, only 3 millimeters long, rests on a blue sea squirt in the coral reefs of Komodo, Indonesia. © Gergo Rugli / Ocean Photographer of the Year Third Place, Human Connection. A teenager stands at Bronte Ocean Pool, Sydney, as a powerful swell sends waves crashing over the closed bathing site. While the conditions forced beaches to shut, people watched the waves from behind the fence. A group of locals climbed into the closed area and stood on the edge, waiting for the waves to crash over them and sweep them across the pool. c© Thomas Pavy / Ocean Photographer of the Year First Place, Conservation Hope. A great hammerhead shark, known as Tamataroa in French Polynesia, is photographed at 55 meters depth in Tiputa Pass, Rangiroa Atoll, during a population survey. This image represents the moment an anonymous shark becomes a known individual. Through photo identification and laser-calibrated video photogrammetry, scientists can track sharks over time to measure their size, sex, and population trends. © Leighton Lum / Ocean Photographer of the Year Finalist, Conservation Hope. A Hawaiian monk seal rests with her week-old pup on Kaimana Beach in Waikīkī. Mothers nurse their pups for around six weeks without feeding, losing up to a third of their body weight while the pup grows before becoming independent. © Lin Yongxuan / Ocean Photographer of the Year Finalist, Conservation Hope. At sunrise, a traditional fishing village shares the coastline with rows of oﬀshore wind turbines stretching across the sea, on Nanri Island, Fujian, China. © James Ferrara / Ocean Photographer of the Year First Place, Conservation Impact. A whale shark is surrounded by divers and snorkelers in the Maldives, revealing the overwhelming pressure that crowded wildlife tourism can place on marine animals. With almost 50 people visible in the frame, this image captures the reality behind some popular wildlife encounters: an animal seeking space while people compete for a closer view. It challenges us to rethink how we experience and protect the species we admire. © Yuta Shigeno / Ocean Photographer of the Year Third Place, Conservation Hope. A male white-spotted puﬀerfish creates an intricate spawning nest in the sand. The fish carefully shapes a two-meter-wide radial pattern using only his fins. Built over several days, this structure and its subtle details reveal the extraordinary eﬀort this small fish invests in reproduction. © Iris Uijttewaal / Ocean Photographer of the Year Finalist, Ocean Unseen. A pygmy seahorse, no larger than a grain of rice, clings to a delicate hydroid in the reefs of Raja Ampat, Indonesia. Perfectly camouflaged, these tiny animals are rarely seen, even by experienced divers. © Daniel Taylor / Ocean Photographer of the Year Finalist, Conservation Impact. A silky shark circles helplessly after taking bait from an illegal longline, its fate sealed by a steel hook and heavy line designed to prevent escape. Photographed less than 48 hours after Baja California’s seasonal shark-fishing ban ended, the image reveals a hidden reality unfolding far from shore. A small group of pilot fish remains beside the shark, highlighting how the loss of one animal can ripple throughout an entire ecosystem. © Chen Lin / Ocean Photographer of the Year Finalist, Human Connection. From above, moored fishing and tourist boats bloom across the sapphire-blue sea, like the petals of a flower. Fringed by golden coastal vegetation, the shoreline becomes an abstract pattern that is diﬃcult to recognize from ground level. © Mitsuna Kawai / Ocean Photographer of the Year First Place, Ocean Unseen. A ribbonfish rises vertically through the dark waters of Osezaki, Japan. Its long, silver body and delicate fins are adapted for life in the open ocean. This image was captured during a winter blackwater dive. Around the ribbonfish, a swarm of salps—small jelly-like animals that feed on tiny particles in the ocean—provides a glimpse of life moving through the deep sea. © Lana Tannir / Ocean Photographer of the Year Finalist, Conservation Hope. Animal care workers perform daily physiotherapy on Norah, a juvenile harbour porpoise undergoing rehabilitation at SOS Dolfijn in the Netherlands. Rescued after being stranding on the Dutch coast, Norah was treated for multiple serious conditions, including pneumonia and severe muscle spasms. This image captures the intensive care required to return her to the sea. To see all of the winning images, be sure to visit Oceanographic Magazine ’s full gallery .

items.title: Profanation du drapeau national dans un hôtel à Alger : peines réduites en appel
items.description: Les peines ont été réduites en appel, mais elles restent lourdes. Les auteurs de la profanation de l’emblème national dans un hôtel de la capitale viennent d'être jugés devant la Cour d'appel d’Alger. Le 8 juin dernier, le tribunal de Bir Mourad Rais a condamné à 7 ans de prison ferme et à 500 000 dinars d’amende deux individus filmés trois jours plus tôt en train de piétiner le drapeau national lors d’un événement au Legacy Luxury Hotel, sis à Hydra (Alger). La vidéo, largement partagée sur les réseaux sociaux, avait choqué l’opinion publique. Profanation du drapeau national : 5 ans de prison ferme pour les mis en cause La Cour d’Alger a rendu ce mercredi 9 septembre son verdict dans le procès en appel de cette affaire. Selon le média Ennahar , la dixième chambre pénale de cette juridiction d'appel a réduit les peines prononcées en première instance et condamné les deux mis en cause, Kh.A.A, organisateur de l’événement, et A.M.S, qui a filmé la scène, à cinq ans de prison ferme, assortis du paiement solidaire de la somme de 20 millions de dinars au Trésor public. Parallèlement à ces poursuites judiciaires, le ministère du Tourisme et de l’Artisanat avait procédé, dès la diffusion de la vidéo, à la fermeture immédiate de l'établissement hôtelier, avec retrait de l'autorisation d'exploitation, pour « atteinte aux symboles de l'État et profanation de l’emblème national » . L’article Profanation du drapeau national dans un hôtel à Alger : peines réduites en appel est apparu en premier sur TSA .

Un chef rebelle condamné à 15 ans de prison ferme
items.description: Le chef rebelle centrafricain Abdoulaye Miskine a été condamné, le mercredi 9 septembre 2026, à 15 ans de prison ferme et au versement de 30 millions de F CFA à chacune des familles des victimes par la cour criminelle de N’Djamena. La justice tchadienne l’a reconnu coupable de plusieurs faits graves liés à des exactions commises dans les zones frontalières entre 2002 et 2003. Le verdict est tombé au palais de justice de N’Djamena. Comme le rapportent plusieurs médias, «la cour criminelle du palais de justice de Ndjamena a déclaré le général Miskine coupable d'association de malfaiteurs, de sévices graves, de torture et d'assassinat». De son vrai nom Martin Koumtamadji, Abdoulaye Miskine est l’ancien patron de la garde présidentielle centrafricaine et le dirigeant du Front démocratique du peuple centrafricain (FDPC). Les faits qui lui sont reprochés, notamment des actes de «torture», d’«assassinat» et de «séquestration», remontent à 2002 et 2003 dans des zones situées à la frontière entre le Tchad et la Centrafrique. Ses trois coaccusés ont également été reconnus coupables, mais en qualité de complices. Ils écopent chacun de 10 ans de prison ferme. Le parquet avait requis 30 ans de réclusion contre Abdoulaye Miskine. La défense, qui plaidait l’acquittement, a rejeté le verdict et annoncé son intention de se pourvoir en cassation. Selon l’Agence de Presse Africaine (APA), les avocats contestent la décision et dénoncent un «jugement politique». Arrêté fin 2019 par les forces tchadiennes, Abdoulaye Miskine était depuis détenu à la maison d’arrêt de Klessoum. Avec cette condamnation, la justice tchadienne tourne une nouvelle page dans un dossier qui traînait depuis plus de deux décennies. Mais le verdict est loin de clore l’affaire, la défense ayant annoncé son recours en cassation, laissant désormais la suite de la procédure entre les mains de la juridiction supérieure. Par Valentin SOMANDE L’article Un chef rebelle condamné à 15 ans de prison ferme est apparu en premier sur Wakat Séra .

items.title: Republicans put Trump centre stage in US midterms gamble
items.description: US Republicans open an extraordinary midterm convention in Dallas on Wednesday, betting that putting Donald Trump at the centre of their campaign can rescue a party facing grim election forecasts — despite the president’s deeply negative approval ratings. The two-day gathering, dubbed “Trumpapalooza,” is designed to persuade the Republican leader’s supporters that he is effectively on the ballot on November 3, when Republicans risk losing the House of Representatives and face a fierce fight to retain the Senate. “So what I really want you to do is pretend, please, that I’m on the ballot,” Trump said recently at a rally in South Carolina. “Just come and vote. It’s so important.” Decision Desk HQ projects Democrats to win the House 230-205 and the Senate to finish 51-49 in their favour — revising its 50-50 prediction as the outlook continues to worsen for Republicans. Trump, whose approval rating stood at just 33 per cent in recent polling , will speak on both convention nights at the American Airlines Centre. U.S. President Donald Trump walks to board Marine One, en route to Dallas, Texas, at the Ellipse near the White House in Washington, DC, the US on September 9, 2026. — Reuters His challenge is to mobilise voters personally loyal to him without further alienating independents already souring on his presidency amid inflation woes, gasoline prices topping $4 a gallon and the continuing war on Iran . “Many Trump supporters only vote when he’s on the ballot,” Matthew Green, a politics professor at the Catholic University of America, told AFP . “They’re not diehard Republican voters; they’re diehard Trump voters. So, in that respect, it makes some sense to feature Trump in the hopes of getting those folks to turn out in November.” But Green was sceptical that asking those supporters to imagine Trump on their ballots could overcome his broader weakness. “When you’re in the low- to mid-30s, that’s traditionally associated with a very bad midterm for your party,” he said of the 80-year-old’s approval ratings. Trump show The gathering is the first Republican national convention held specifically for a midterm election, although no candidates will be nominated and no formal party business is planned. Instead, organisers have constructed what amounts to a two-night television rally touting Trump’s record and Republican candidates. More than 100 House members and candidates are expected, with over 50 speakers or presentations scheduled each night. Rubber ducks shaped as US President Donald Trump are seen at a store outside of the American Airlines Centre ahead of the 2026 Republican National Committee (RNC) Midterm Convention in Dallas, Texas on September 08, 2026. — AFP Trump delivers Wednesday’s keynote and returns for Thursday’s finale after Vice President JD Vance speaks. Cabinet members, congressional leaders and candidates in closely watched House and Senate races are also on the program. Republicans plan to highlight tax cuts, immigration enforcement, manufacturing and prescription drug prices, while depicting Democrats as dangerously far to the left. Some Republicans, however, are privately hoping Trump sticks to that script rather than the personal grievances and off-message subjects that regularly dominate his appearances. Staying home Not everyone is coming. Numerous lawmakers in competitive races have decided that, less than two months from Election Day, their time is better spent campaigning at home. House Speaker Mike Johnson has acknowledged the dilemma, saying some members need to remain home because it is a “critical time” immediately before early voting accelerates nationwide. And even Trump’s promised national television showcase faces an unusually formidable rival. Both convention nights coincide with the opening games of the NFL season. “Spending three or four days away from your district to go to a convention is not a good way to spend your time if you’re facing a tight re-election,” Green added. Democrats were also making their presence felt in Dallas, with the party sending out some of its most high-profile speakers for public events. “Americans are being crushed by rising costs,” Colorado Congressman Jason Crow posted on X. “Republicans don’t care — they’re in Dallas, celebrating an out-of-touch President whose tariffs and wars are making things worse. We’re going to hold them accountable.”

items.title: Tongue routs Pakistan as England dominate in third Test
items.description: England are on course to complete a series whitewash after Pakistan’s brittle batting collapsed again on the opening day of the third Test at Edgbaston on Wednesday. The tourists, who have failed to reach 200 in the series, were dismantled once more by England’s four-man pace attack and were shot out for 133 in just 33.5 overs. Josh Tongue led the way with 4-42 with Ollie Robinson taking 3-15 and Jofra Archer 3-25. Debutant Razaullah enjoyed a dream start to his Pakistan test career, taking the prize wicket of Joe Root with his fourth ball, but a century stand from Emilio Gay and Harry Brook put England in command. They closed with a lead of 23 on 156-4. Razaullah, 21, was one of three new caps, along with wicketkeeper Ghazi Ghori and Mohammad Imran, in a Pakistan side thrown into chaos when seven players were sent home after the second test loss at Lords. Coach Sarfaraz Ahmed and his assistant Umar Gul were also sacked in the aftermath. The pattern of the series was maintained with Pakistan getting away to another awful start after being put in to bat, slumping to 26-4 inside the opening hour. Saim Ayub, recalled after a 21-month absence, was trapped lbw by Robinson, giving the Sussex captain his 100th Test wicket in his 24th test, and opening partner Azan Awais was caught by a diving Tongue at wide mid-on off Archer for nine. Abdullah Shafique followed, caught well low down to his left at gully by Dan Lawrence off Robinson for three. When Shan Masood miscued a pull to mid-on off Archer, the tourists were reeling. Pakistan’s problems mounted when Tongue was introduced. He bowled Pakistan captain Babar Azam in his first over for seven, trapped Ghazi for four before yorking Imran for five. At lunch Pakistan were in disarray at 100-7. Razaullah lasted just three balls after the resumption, edging Robinson to Ben Duckett who made amends for two earlier spills with the catch. Saud Shakeel, who hit 97 at Lords, top-scored again with 43 from 47 balls before becoming Tongue’s fourth victim. It said much about Pakistan’s limp effort that the highest partnership of the innings was the last-wicket stand of 26 between Mohammad Abbas, who made 21, and Mohammad Ali. England did not have it all their own way when their turn came on a surface offering some help to the bowlers with Ali and Abbas nipping out Duckett and Jordan Cox respectively early on. When Root fell lbw for the ninth time in his last 12 test innings, England were 39-3 but Brook and Gay restored order. For Gay, still establishing himself in the England side, his highest Test score of 60 from 114 balls was an important contribution. He exited late on, dragging on a ball from the impressive Razaullah, who touched 90mph, but Brook will be at the crease on 52 tomorrow morning alongside Lawrence.

items.title: Mines : la Guinée pose les bases d’un Fonds souverain doté de 4 milliards USD entre 2029 et 2035
items.description: La Guinée veut transformer une partie des revenus tirés de ses ressources minières en investissements durables et en épargne pour les générations futures. Le gouvernement a présenté, ce mercredi 9 septembre 2026, les grandes orientations du futur Fonds souverain de Guinée (FSG), appelé notamment à accompagner le Programme Simandou 2040. Réunis autour du Premier ministre Amadou Oury Bah et de la ministre de l’Économie, des Finances et du Budget, Mariama Ciré Sylla, des membres du gouvernement, cadres de l’administration, représentants du secteur privé, partenaires techniques et financiers et experts ont examiné l’architecture envisagée pour cette nouvelle institution. Selon les éléments présentés par le directeur du Bureau de stratégie et de développement (BSD), Mamadou Saliou Diallo, le Fonds devrait être constitué sous la forme d’une société anonyme à capitaux publics, détenue à 100 % par l’État. Les projections prévoient 4 milliards de dollars de dotations entre 2029 et 2035. L’objectif affiché est de rendre le Fonds opérationnel dès 2026, parallèlement à la montée en puissance des exportations de minerai de fer de Simandou. Trois missions : investir, stabiliser et épargner Le dispositif envisagé repose sur trois compartiments distincts. Le premier sera consacré à l’investissement et au développement, notamment dans la transformation minière, l’agro-industrie, les infrastructures productives et l'émergence de champions nationaux. Le deuxième aura une fonction de stabilisation. Il devra permettre d’amortir les conséquences de la volatilité des cours des matières premières sur les recettes publiques. Enfin, un compartiment d’épargne intergénérationnelle devra constituer progressivement un patrimoine diversifié, notamment à l’international, destiné à survivre à l’épuisement des ressources minières. Pour Mariama Ciré Sylla, l'enjeu consiste précisément à éviter que l'exploitation actuelle des ressources épuisables ne bénéficie qu'aux générations présentes. « Une partie des revenus de nos ressources naturelles sera préservée au bénéfice de ceux qui viendront après nous. C'est peut-être la dimension la plus exigeante de ce projet : accepter de mettre de côté aujourd'hui pour que demain soit plus solide », a-t-elle déclaré. La ministre a également insisté sur la vocation de développement du mécanisme. Les revenus miniers, a-t-elle soutenu, devront se traduire notamment par des infrastructures, des services de santé et d'éducation ainsi que des emplois. Raffineries, aciérie et agro-industrie parmi les investissements envisagés Les premières pistes présentées donnent une place importante à la transformation locale des matières premières. Figurent notamment parmi les projets envisagés des raffineries d'alumine, une aciérie d'une capacité de 500 000 tonnes par an et une raffinerie d'or d'une capacité annoncée de 250 000 à 500 000 kilogrammes par an. Le dispositif pourrait également soutenir des parcs agro-industriels utilisant les infrastructures du corridor de Simandou, une école de formation en alumine à Conakry, la modernisation de l'Institut supérieur des mines et de la géologie de Boké ainsi que le renforcement des capacités des PME guinéennes. Agriculture, élevage, pêche, santé, éducation et formation à travers la Simandou Academy, mais également tourisme, culture et artisanat apparaissent aussi dans les domaines susceptibles de bénéficier des investissements. Le Fonds est présenté comme l'un des instruments financiers devant accompagner Simandou 2040, programme comprenant, selon les données exposées, 122 mégaprojets, 36 réformes et plus de 200 milliards de dollars d'investissements projetés à l'horizon 2040, dont plus de 65 milliards durant la phase d'accélération 2025-2030. Le FSG n'a toutefois pas vocation à financer à lui seul ces 200 milliards de dollars. Il est plutôt présenté comme un outil destiné à mobiliser et attirer d'autres capitaux autour de projets jugés rentables sur les plans économique, social et financier. « Il investit, il ne dépense pas » Les concepteurs insistent également sur ce que le futur Fonds ne devra pas devenir. Il ne s'agira ni d'une caisse dans laquelle l'État pourra puiser librement en cas de difficulté budgétaire, ni d'un guichet de subventions. Le principe présenté est celui d'un investisseur de long terme : chaque franc engagé devra générer un retour sous forme de dividendes, de remboursement ou de création de valeur. Les financements pourront s'étendre sur 10, 15 ou 20 ans, contre des horizons généralement plus courts pour les banques commerciales. Le FSG pourrait investir aux côtés d'acteurs privés guinéens ou étrangers afin de partager les risques et de mobiliser des financements supplémentaires. Bah Oury met en garde contre les pressions du court terme Dans son intervention, le Premier ministre a surtout insisté sur la discipline qui devra entourer la gestion de cette institution. « Les ressources issues du Simandou ne devront jamais être absorbées par les seules urgences du présent », a averti Amadou Oury Bah. Elles devront, selon lui, soutenir la diversification économique, renforcer les capacités d'investissement du pays et préserver une partie de la richesse nationale au profit des générations futures. Le chef du gouvernement demande notamment des règles précises concernant les versements et les retraits, une gouvernance reposant sur la compétence et la responsabilité ainsi qu'une publication régulière des informations relatives à la gestion du Fonds. « Les ressources qui lui seront confiées appartiennent à la Nation. Leur gestion devra pouvoir être justifiée, documentée et évaluée », a-t-il insisté. Cette question de gouvernance constitue l'un des principaux enjeux du projet. Le gouvernement annonce vouloir aligner le FSG sur les principes de Santiago, référentiel international de bonnes pratiques applicable aux fonds souverains. Comment les projets seront-ils sélectionnés ? Le mécanisme présenté prévoit plusieurs étapes avant qu'un projet ne bénéficie d'un investissement : vérification de son éligibilité, analyse des risques opérationnels, financiers et juridiques, examen de sa rentabilité et de son impact, structuration du financement, approbation puis suivi. Les secteurs prioritaires cités comprennent notamment la transformation manufacturière et métallurgique, l'agriculture et l'agro-industrie, le BTP et le logement, la logistique et les transports, l'énergie et l'eau, le tourisme, le numérique et l'industrie financière. Pour les opérations les plus importantes, celles dépassant 5 % du bilan du Fonds, l'approbation relèverait du conseil d'administration. En dessous de ce seuil, la décision pourrait être déléguée à la direction exécutive. À l'issue de l'atelier, le gouvernement entend désormais consolider le cadre juridique et institutionnel, préciser la doctrine d'investissement et arrêter la feuille de route devant conduire à l'opérationnalisation du Fonds. Pour Bah Oury, la réussite du mécanisme se mesurera surtout sur le long terme : « Notre génération sera jugée sur l'usage qu'elle aura fait des ressources exceptionnelles confiées à la Guinée. »

items.title: Le Roi Mohammed VI condamne « l’agression criminelle iranienne » contre la Jordanie
items.description: Le Roi Mohammed VI a adressé, selon un communiqué du Cabinet royal, un message de solidarité et de condamnation au Roi Abdallah II Ibn Al Hussein, Souverain du Royaume hachémite de Jordanie, à la suite des attaques iraniennes répétées visant le pays frère. Dans son message, le Souverain affirme : « J’ai suivi avec une profonde préoccupation et indignation la nouvelle des attaques de missiles iraniennes, qui ont ciblé le territoire du Royaume hachémite de Jordanie frère, dans le prolongement de l’attitude hostile de l’Iran à l’égard de votre pays frère ainsi que des États arabes du Golfe. » « Face à cet événement grave, je tiens à exprimer à Votre Majesté ma ferme condamnation et mon profond rejet de cette agression criminelle et injustifiée, qui vise à porter atteinte à la stabilité de votre pays frère et à semer la terreur et l’inquiétude quant à la sécurité et à l’intégrité du peuple jordanien » , poursuit le Roi Mohammed VI. Le Souverain réaffirme également « la solidarité absolue du Royaume du Maroc avec le Royaume hachémite de Jordanie frère et son soutien constant et inconditionnel à toutes les mesures prises par les autorités jordaniennes, sous votre sage conduite, pour défendre la sécurité et la stabilité de la Jordanie ainsi que la sécurité de ses citoyens ». Le Roi Mohammed VI souligne à cet égard que « la sécurité de la Jordanie est partie intégrante de celle du Maroc ». En conclusion, le Souverain fait part de sa confiance dans le fait que « le peuple jordanien, sous votre conduite éclairée, saura surmonter les conséquences de ces attaques criminelles, grâce à la détermination, à la solidarité et au sang-froid qui le caractérisent ». The post Le Roi Mohammed VI condamne « l’agression criminelle iranienne » contre la Jordanie appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Kafra : le Niger avance avec prudence vers un nouveau potentiel pétrolier…
items.description: Niamey, 9 septembre 2026 – Le Niger entend poursuivre l’évaluation du bloc pétrolier de Kafra avec « prudence, transparence et détermination », afin de transformer son potentiel en une source durable de souveraineté énergétique, de recettes et d’emplois au profit des Nigériens, a déclaré mercredi le ministre du Pétrole, Hamadou Tini. Lors d’un point de presse consacré à la campagne de forage lancée le 13 février 2026, le ministre a rappelé que le programme en cours prévoit le forage de quatre puits d’exploration sur une période de deux ans. Cette phase s’inscrit dans une autorisation d’exploration prorogée jusqu’au 3 juillet 2028. « Il serait prématuré de donner aujourd’hui une date certaine du premier baril », a prévenu M. Tini. Selon lui, une éventuelle mise en production dépendra notamment des résultats des forages, de la confirmation des volumes, de la productivité des réservoirs, de la faisabilité technique, des infrastructures à réaliser et des financements à mobiliser. Le gouvernement, a-t-il assuré, veut avancer rapidement, mais sans précipitation. « Dans le pétrole, une mauvaise décision prise très tôt peut coûter beaucoup plus cher qu’une bonne décision prise au bon moment », a souligné le ministre. Les travaux déjà réalisés sur le bloc de Kafra ont permis d’identifier plusieurs découvertes et un potentiel pétrolier jugé important. Les réserves 2P liées à une découverte effectuée sur le bloc avaient été estimées à environ 255 millions de barils en 2018. Une étude prospective conduite en 2023 dans la partie nord du bloc a, par ailleurs, évalué les ressources prospectives à environ 2,5 milliards de barils. Le ministre a toutefois insisté sur le caractère encore hypothétique de ce chiffre, soumis aux incertitudes géologiques et aux risques propres à l’exploration. « Kafra est encore dans une phase d’exploration et d’évaluation », a-t-il expliqué, précisant que les quatre puits programmés doivent fournir des données supplémentaires sur la qualité des réservoirs, leur étendue, leur productivité et la viabilité économique d’un futur développement. Le site recèle également un réservoir distinct d’huile lourde, dont les volumes sont estimés, sous réserve d’études complémentaires, à près de 168 millions de barils. Ce potentiel pourrait, à terme, contribuer à l’alimentation d’une unité de production de bitume destinée aux marchés nigérien et régional des matériaux routiers. Le bloc présente aussi un potentiel d’huile paraffinique susceptible d’intéresser les filières pharmaceutiques et pétrochimiques. Pour Hamadou Tini, l’enjeu de Kafra dépasse la seule perspective d’une production de pétrole. Le projet doit contribuer à la création de valeur nationale, à travers l’application de la loi sur le contenu local, le transfert de compétences, le renforcement des entreprises nigériennes et la maîtrise progressive des données et savoir-faire du secteur. « Avec Kafra, le Niger n’attend pas seulement un nombre de barils, nous attendons une création de valeur nationale », a affirmé le ministre. Les volumes officiels actualisés ne seront communiqués qu’après consolidation, certification et validation des résultats techniques et économiques, conformément aux normes reconnues dans l’industrie pétrolière. Le projet Kafra est localisé dans la zone désertique du nord du Niger, dans la région d’Agadez, entre les départements d’Iferouane et de Bilma, à environ 85 kilomètres de la frontière sud de l’Algérie. Le bloc, qui couvre 11 467 kilomètres carrés, abrite notamment le puits d’exploration Kafra Sud-Est 1. L’exploration pétrolière dans cette zone remonte aux années 1970, avec les forages historiques de Séguédine 1 en 1974 et de Tiffa 1 en 1975. Depuis 2005, Sipex, filiale du groupe algérien Sonatrach, participe aux activités sur le bloc. Les travaux ont permis l’acquisition, le traitement et l’interprétation d’environ 2 205 kilomètres de données sismiques 2D et de 760 kilomètres carrés de sismique 3D. Deux puits d’exploration ont ensuite été forés en 2018 et 2019, avant l’actualisation du cadre du projet en 2022. La prorogation de l’autorisation d’exploration et le lancement de la nouvelle campagne de quatre forages marquent ainsi une nouvelle étape dans l’évaluation du potentiel de Kafra. L’ambition affichée par les autorités est que ce projet génère des emplois, des recettes, des compétences et de nouvelles opportunités pour les Nigériens, dans le cadre d’une coopération renforcée avec l’Algérie. Source : Ministère du Pétrole et ANP L’article Kafra : le Niger avance avec prudence vers un nouveau potentiel pétrolier… est apparu en premier sur Tamtaminfo .

items.title: Droits des femmes : Le féminicide et l’avortement médicalisé au cœur des échanges avec le ministre de la Justice
items.description: Le ministre de la Justice, Garde des Sceaux, Me Moussa Sarr, a reçu, lundi 7 septembre 2026, une délégation d’organisations féminines et féministes. Les échanges ont porté sur plusieurs revendications relatives aux droits des femmes et des filles, notamment la reconnaissance du féminicide, la réforme du Code de la famille et l’avortement médicalisé en cas de viol et d’inceste. La question des droits des femmes s’est invitée, lundi, au ministère de la Justice. Me Moussa Sarr, Garde des Sceaux, a reçu une délégation composée de plusieurs organisations féminines et féministes engagées dans la défense et la promotion des droits des femmes et des filles. Parmi les participantes figuraient notamment Aminata Diallo, représentant Actrices Culturelles Ensemble (ACE), Maïmouna Yade et Oussama Sagna de J-Gen Sénégal, la sociologue Selly Ba, des représentantes du Réseau des Féministes du Sénégal et du Collectif des Féministes du Sénégal. Des organisations telles que l’Association des juristes sénégalaises (AJS), le Collectif Dafadoy, Roajelf, Pencum Ndakarou et Libéra étaient également représentées. La rencontre a permis aux organisations de présenter les travaux préparatoires aux assises nationales envisagées sur les droits des femmes et des filles. Elles ont également plaidé pour l’instauration d’un cadre permanent de dialogue et de concertation entre l’État et les organisations de la société civile. Le féminicide au cœur des revendications Plusieurs préoccupations ont été soulevées au cours des échanges. Les organisations ont notamment demandé la reconnaissance du féminicide comme une infraction autonome, au regard de la spécificité des violences meurtrières visant les femmes. La refonte du Code de la famille ainsi que l’accès à l’avortement médicalisé dans les cas de viol et d’inceste ont également figuré parmi les principaux sujets abordés. La situation des femmes détenues, les violences faites aux femmes et aux enfants et le harcèlement, notamment en ligne, ont aussi été évoqués. Les représentantes ont, par ailleurs, insisté sur la nécessité de renforcer la prise en charge des victimes et la formation des forces de sécurité. Elles ont salué l’action des Maisons de Justice, tout en appelant à leur affecter davantage de moyens. « Une attention particulière » aux préoccupations En réponse aux différentes préoccupations, Me Moussa Sarr a assuré qu’elles feraient l’objet d’une attention particulière. Il a notamment annoncé que la question des violences faites aux femmes et aux filles sera prise en compte dans le cadre de la circulaire de politique pénale générale. Sur la reconnaissance du féminicide, le ministre s’est déclaré, « a priori », favorable à une consécration spécifique de cette infraction. Les questions relatives à la réforme du Code de la famille et à l’avortement médicalisé en cas de viol et d’inceste appellent, selon le Garde des Sceaux, davantage de réflexion. Il a souligné le caractère sensible de ces sujets et appelé à poursuivre les échanges afin de parvenir à des « compromis dynamiques » prenant en compte les différentes opinions au sein de la société sénégalaise. Vers un cadre permanent de concertation Me Moussa Sarr a également réaffirmé la volonté de son département de considérer les organisations de défense des droits humains comme des « partenaires privilégiés de l’État ». Dans cette perspective, il a annoncé la mise en place prochaine d’un cadre de concertation et de dialogue réunissant les organisations de défense des droits humains au moins une fois par an. L’objectif sera notamment de faire le point sur la situation des droits humains au Sénégal. Le ministre a, en outre, évoqué l’étude d’un comité ad hoc chargé de préparer une stratégie nationale en matière de droits humains. La rencontre s’est achevée sur la volonté partagée de poursuivre le dialogue autour de la protection et de la promotion des droits des femmes et des filles. Arame NDIAYE

items.title: Govt hikes petrol price by Rs3.40, diesel by Rs6.72
items.description: Pakistan fuel prices, 2026 Official ex-depot prices (PKR/litre) — OGRA & Ministry of Energy notifications Petrol (MS-92) Diesel (HSD) Pre-crisis baseline Source: OGRA / Ministry of Energy (Petroleum Division); Dawn.com · "> The government on Wednesday increased the price of petrol by Rs3.40 per litre and that of high-speed diesel (HSD) by Rs6.72 per litre. Following the revision, petrol will retail at Rs367.75 per litre while HSD will cost Rs392.67 per litre. The government continues to levy Rs114 per litre in taxes and duties on petrol and Rs100 per litre on diesel. According to the Petroleum Division’s notification, the new prices will be applicable on Sept 10 (Thursday). The price of HSD has come down from a peak of Rs520.35 recorded on April 3. Its price had started rising from Rs281 per litre after the US-Iran war broke out on February 28. The petrol price had peaked at Rs458.41 on April 3 after beginning its upward trajectory from Rs266 in the first week of March. On July 17, Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik announced that fuel prices would now be fixed on a daily basis due to fluctuations in international market prices following renewed hostilities between Iran and the US. Prior to this, the government had been announcing weekly revisions to fuel prices since early March, alongside measures for the conservation of fuel amid possible oil supply disruptions due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. The federal government in April also announced targeted relief measures to provide subsidised fuel. The petroleum minister stated that the cabinet and the prime minister had decided to give the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra) the responsibility of deciding fuel prices on a daily basis based on international market trends. Petrol is mainly used in private transport, small vehicles, rickshaws and two-wheelers, and changes in its price affect the middle and lower-middle classes. Similarly, changes in diesel prices also impact the public at large, as it is mainly used in the heavy transport sector, power plants and large generators. Petrol and high-speed diesel (HSD) are the major revenue earners, with monthly sales of about 700,000 to 800,000 tonnes, compared to just 10,000 tonnes of monthly demand for kerosene.

items.title: Inside the White House on 9/11
items.description: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube In this episode of The David Frum Show , The Atlantic ’s David Frum is joined by John McConnell, the longtime senior speechwriter for President George W. Bush and Vice President Dick Cheney, to discuss their memories of September 11, 2001—25 years later. Then, David ends with a discussion of American Pastoral, a novel by Philip Roth, and what we can learn about domestic terrorism from the book. The following is a transcript of the episode: David Frum: Well, what I remember, that’s actually maybe one of my most vivid memories of the day, is stepping out of that building and Washington is deserted, and there’s yellow tape everywhere marking off the streets, and there’s the National Guard and armored personnel carriers everywhere. But the flags are still flying. They’ll be lowered the next—I remember thinking, They will be lowered tomorrow. But tonight they’re high. [ Music ] Frum: Hello, and welcome to The David Frum Show. I’m David Frum, a staff writer at The Atlantic. My guest this week will be John McConnell, a colleague of mine in the George W. Bush speechwriting department, and himself chief speechwriter to former Vice President Dick Cheney. We’ll be talking about 9/11 at the quarter-century anniversary. John and I spent much of the day together on 9/11, 2001—and we’ll be discussing what we saw, what we thought, what we felt, and what we did. The book discussion this week will also be terrorism-related: the novel American Pastoral by Philip Roth, his discussion of a homegrown terrorist in Roth’s own native state of New Jersey. Before either the dialogue or the book discussion, some home news. We’re going to be conducting an experiment here in The David Frum Show with a new tempo. Twice a week: releasing one show on Wednesday, the show you see, which will contain an interview and a book discussion, and a shorter show, which we’ll be releasing each Saturday on both YouTube and on whatever audio platform you use: Spotify, Apple, whatever it is. The second show, the Saturday show, will be much shorter—no interview, just some thoughts from me on the events of the week just passed. And the first of the shows, which we’ll release this coming Saturday, I will offer my own reflections on the 25th anniversary of 9/11. The United States has been almost unceasingly at war in the Middle East since 9/11, 2001. And I’ll be offering some of my thoughts about how I think about that experience, how others might want to think about it, whatever information I can offer. I played a small part in that history, and I think about it almost all the time, and I’ll be sharing those thoughts with you. And we’ll be continuing each Saturday after that. I do hope you’ll join and will bookmark us or subscribe to The Atlantic YouTube channel, or whatever audio channel you use, so you will not miss any of our Saturday shows. So that’s the news. I hope you will join me this coming Saturday and each successive Saturday for the second, shorter David Frum Show weekend episode. And now my dialogue with John McConnell. [ Music ] Frum: My guest today is John McConnell. John is one of the greatest speechwriters in American history, but that’s only incidentally why I’ve invited him today. John was a colleague in the George W. Bush administration, and I spent much of September 11th, 2001, in his company, sharing emotions of shock, dismay, and grief. As we mark the 25th anniversary of a tragic day, I wanted to be with him again. John wrote for Vice President Dan Quayle, then for the Bob Dole for President campaign in 1996. He joined the George W. Bush campaign in 2000 and then did remarkable service in the Bush White House, where he doubled as both a writer for the president and the sole speechwriter for Vice President Richard Cheney. John was a pallbearer at Vice President Cheney’s funeral. It was his frequent writing partner, Matt Scully, who delivered the finest verdict on John’s work: “As a general rule in Bush speeches, if the writing is graceful, judicious, and understated and makes you think about the subject at hand instead of anyone’s particular craftsmanship or religiosity, there’s a better-than-even chance it is by John McConnell.” It’s John’s lifelong reflex to deflect attention from himself, but today he must overcome that reflex and accept his place in American history. Thank you, John, for joining me today. John McConnell: Hello, David. Great to see you. Frum: So we spent the day together on 9/11. Let me start by asking you to summon your memories of what happened that day, where you were at, from the beginning to the end. McConnell: I was sitting outside Vice President Cheney’s inner office door in the West Wing. The night before, Matthew Scully and I had been working on a speech for the president for the end of that week. And at the end of Monday, I looked at my list of things to do, and I realized that Cheney had a speech on Friday too, and I thought, Well, I haven’t given this much thought. I should go talk to him. So I called his secretary. I said, Can I pop in on him tomorrow morning? And she said, How much time do you need? I said, Ten minutes, maybe five. I just wanted to ask him about his speech. And she said, Sure. Come at 8:30. And so the next morning—you remember how we’d get to the office, and the president’s and vice president’s schedules would be under our doors. And I looked at it; it said, “Meeting with John McConnell, 8:30,” and I thought, Oh, well, it’s an official meeting, so I really better be there at 8:30 sharp. So I went over, and the vice president was there. And anyway, what the president said after the events—he said, Night fell on a different world. Frum: Yeah. So it’s about 8:00 at night. We get into the White House. Again, and it’s a different White House. Because the security—although there was security before 9/11, a lot of security—it was different after. And it was already, it was instantly different. So we didn’t go watch the president speak, which is what I think we normally would’ve done. Again, there were just many more barriers to moving around inside. And the president spoke to the nation, but still in a way that was a little punch drunk, in my opinion. And I looked this up later. So, after the firing on Fort Sumter, President Lincoln’s first communication to the nation is a written proclamation that he issued three days after the firing on Fort Sumter. And after the attack on Pearl Harbor, President Roosevelt’s first communication to the nation was his Day of Infamy speech. But Pearl Harbor was struck at dawn Hawaii time, which on Sunday, which is about midday Washington time Sunday. And the president spoke first thing Monday. So however many hours that is before the first communication. In—it’s not yet the social-media age, but it’s the cable-TV age, and the president has to speak the same day, immediately. And in a way, there isn’t really time. That isn’t enough time to organize what you’re going to say. And so even the 8:00 speech struck me as not the right tone, not the right message exactly. McConnell: Well, and then it was Monday the 17th where we got the assignment to do the speech to Congress on Thursday. And that was, of course, that would be then September 20th. It was nine days after the events in question. And if you look at history, it feels like a long time. But he did have the speech at the National Cathedral on Friday, and the radio address. Which I don’t even remember what that— Frum: Well, I want to put a break—again, I want to slow down here a little bit, because here are the things I remember that are signal events before the speech to Congress. There’s the speech to the National Cathedral, as you said, which was, I thought, so—that was beautiful. This is not my own work. I’ll say, because my portfolio was domestic and economic, so I was spending all my time on, like, the stock market and the reopening of the airlines. So the speeches I’m about to praise, I had nothing to do with. That beautiful speech at the National Cathedral, which I think you and Scully mostly wrote. And then he went to New York to speak at Ground Zero. And that famous moment, “I can hear you,” that was, as far as I’m aware, completely improvised in the moment. And then—and I think this is the thing, I think, people don’t remember enough—that he went to the Washington mosque on Massachusetts Avenue, I think, again, before the speech to Congress. And stood with dignitaries local and national, and made a speech for tolerance. And I just want to stress this point, because there is a lot of misremembering and I think a lot of misinformation about what it was like to belong to the American Muslim community after 9/11. There were a flurry of hate attacks after 9/11, in the immediate aftermath of 9/11. I remember, in fact, I think three of them were murders. Two of the murders were carried out by the same person. And the three victims—only one of the three was Muslim; one was Sikh, and one was South Asian of non-Muslim background. And then many other incidents of harassment and intimidation and insult and vandalism. But the president was so forceful condemning it that that flurry of hate-crime incidents—and three of them murders in the immediate aftermath—was quickly stopped. And there is a dramatic drop-off between, after the month of September into October. I think the killings were in September and October. By January of 2002, the FBI is recording a steep drop, I think, of hate-crime incidents, from that last half of 2001. And that the leadership of President Bush and people like him really made an important difference in creating an atmosphere of tolerance and respect that is not as remembered as well as it should be. McConnell: Well, that’s a nice point, David. And this is a great country, and no patriot is going to want to harm an innocent, unsuspecting person in response to something like this. I mean, this is the horror of 9/11, is that very thing: harming innocent, unsuspecting people. And President Bush in that sense spoke for the best in our country and brought out the best, as I like to think he always did, and I know that he tried to do. Frum: Well, again, to conjure it up, so—President Bush is kind of an accidental president in a way. He lost the popular vote in the election of 2000. He becomes president, he wins the electoral vote, and everything teeters on the state of Florida, where, on a few dozen votes in the state of Florida—because in those days, every county got to design its own ballot, and many of the counties did a bad job. And there was recount upon recount, and tremendous ill feeling about it. And it left behind, I think, a shadow. I know he spent a lot of the first half of 2001 trying to find ways to broaden his support. There is an emphasis on education as an early initiative, because that had broad bipartisan support. You could pass it with big majorities of both Republicans and Democrats in both houses of Congress. But still, there was a question mark over his presidency up to that moment. And I think there was this feeling of—would he measure up? Could this accidental president be someone who could speak for the nation after 9/11? McConnell: Well, that’s right. And I remember Bob Dole candidly said, some months after that, he said—I think he was talking about September 14th, when Bush was on that flattened fire truck in New York City with the bullhorn, and didn’t even know he was expected to speak and had nothing prepared for him. And then had one of the iconic moments of his presidency—and Bob Dole said, that was like a second inauguration. ( Laughs .) And it really was the man meeting his moment, and people getting a sense of him that they really hadn’t had or allowed. Or, in the case of many Americans, allowed themselves to have at that time. Frum: Well, on his way to that moment, he landed in New York, and he was taken in a car to Lower Manhattan. And the emergency workers there are the firefighters, and a lot of, not onlookers because the area’s closed to the public, but there were a lot of people there. And they’re all cheering and waving and clapping and greeting him enthusiastically. And Mayor Giuliani, who was in the car with Bush—and Mayor Giuliani was a very different man in 9/11 from the man he is now—and I later heard that he had said to the president, You see all these people cheering for you? Not one of them voted for you. McConnell: Well, and President Bush—you’ve heard him tell the story, David, and he repeated it in his book. He has a strong emotional memory of just one guy in a hard hat standing on a mound of rubble, making eye contact with him, and pointing his finger and said, “Don’t you let me down.” Frum: ( Laughs .) McConnell: And it really, really touched his heart and stays with him to this day. Frum: All right. So we have just a few minutes left. I want to flash forward; now look back on this from the perspective of 25 years. How did the country do? How did the Bush administration do? What did we get right? What did we get wrong? Do you have thoughts looking backward from a perspective of a quarter century on 9/11, and what it meant and what it led to? McConnell: Nothing deep or profound. I grew up in the ’70s and ’80s. I remember once when I was about nine or 10 years old—I grew up in a town of 500 people in northern Wisconsin, and I have this memory of walking with one of my little friends around this little town on a summer day. And we agreed that we were probably never going to see a war in our lifetimes, because people, they don’t do this anymore. You know what I mean? That’s how things felt in the mid- to late ’70s. People aren’t going to fight wars anymore, big tanks and armies and all this stuff. And we just looked ahead to a future where that kind of tragedy and sorrow just wouldn’t fall on the human race like it used to. This is, you know, innocent kid stuff, right? And the ’80s were pretty quiet. And you had the Cold War, but it’s a pretty, pretty quiet decade when you think about it. And so the point is—when 9/11 happened, that was very jarring for me, as it was for everybody. And you get this sense that the world—we might see a lot of things like this from now on, and we might see a lot of things like this inside the United States. That was my biggest fear, that the United States would, having found itself vulnerable that day, would continue to be. I didn’t think we had to be, but I was afraid that we might be. And so when I look back, I think mainly of the president you and I worked for, and the responsibilities that we had. And there’s only so much that speechwriters can do. There’s only so much that’s on the page, and the rest is up to him. And when he did such a great job in those moments, it’s really because of him and the kind of man he was. And this was, as I said before, a man meeting his moment. And our country has not descended into the kind of fright and vulnerability that many of us feared could happen, and that’s not by accident. A lot of good decisions were made; a lot of difficult decisions were made that kept us safe. We could talk about any number of particulars and wars and things of that nature that have come since. But by and large, I look back on that time as a pivotal point, a moment of great decision. And things were handled well by the people in power. Frum: I will have a somewhat different view, which I’ll present on a later occasion. I’ll say just one thing as I think back on it. I think there are many might-have-beens in history, and I’m not a big believer in these alternative scenarios, because usually things that have big consequences don’t have happenstance causes. If the guns firing at Fort Sumter had missed, the Civil War would still have happened. But one I do think about is, if [Osama] bin Laden had not got away in Tora Bora in December of 2001, if the United States and Britain and the many other allies who were there, and the Afghan partners of the United States—if they had succeeded in cornering him and killing him in Tora Bora at the end of 2001, would we have had the quarter century of wars in the Middle East that have since happened? His getting away caused an upping of the ante of American policy. The United States had to do something, and had failed to do in December 2001 the most necessary and logical and demanded thing. And so, sometimes when you fail to solve a problem, you redefine the problem to make the problem bigger. It’s September 11th, 2026. The United States is at war with Iran; American troops have been engaged in anti-terrorist and counterterrorist operations all over the planet for a quarter century. The death toll has been high for Americans, and even higher for others. And I think that 9/11 of 2001 put us on this path. There was an exit in December of 2001, and we didn’t take the exit. We missed the exit. Not through anyone’s fault, or not through anyone’s intention. Maybe somebody’s fault. Not through anyone’s intention. We missed the exit, and here we are. And we’ll be talking about that more in the coming weeks. And John, I thank you so much. Not only did I spend that day with you, I remember also very vividly spending my last day at the White House with you. We had lunch that day, and I remember going with you to the big bow in the South Lawn, the iron fence, and looking out and thinking, All my life I’ve wanted to look into this fence. I’ve had a year and a half of looking out of the fence, and now I’m looking out of it for the last time, with my good friend McConnell by my side. And for the rest of my life, I’ll be back to looking inside and trying to make sense of this with everyone else’s eyes of looking in. But you, you’ve spent so much of your life inside, and your knowledge is so profound, and your heart is so big, and it was an honor to work with you and to be your friend. McConnell: Thank you, David. It was an honor to be your colleague as well. It was a great time, and we’re so privileged to have had that experience. Frum: Bye-bye. McConnell: Thank you. [ Music ] Frum: Thanks so much to my friend John McConnell for joining me today on The David Frum Show. This week’s book is also a contemplation of terrorism, but in this case, a contemplation of homegrown, domestic American terrorism. The book is American Pastoral by Philip Roth, published in 1997. In my opinion, probably his greatest novel. American Pastoral tells a story of an American Jew whose daughter gets mixed up in extremist activity. The novel is narrated by a man named Nathan Zuckerman, who’s Roth’s recurring literary alter ego. And Nathan Zuckerman tells a story of his childhood friend, Seymour “The Swede” Levov, a golden-boy athlete from Zuckerman and Roth’s hometown of Newark, New Jersey. The Swede seems to have it all. He’s a former high-school sports star. He marries a Miss New Jersey. He takes over his father’s successful glove-manufacturing business, and he settles into an idyllic life in rural Old Rimrock, New Jersey. He has one child, an adored daughter named Merry, M-E-R-R-Y. Merry becomes increasingly politically outspoken in the course of the 1960s, when the novel is set. She gets involved in radical causes. She becomes increasingly dogmatic. Merry has a speech impediment, and somehow that concentrates her rage into forms of action that are beyond speech. And ultimately, that expressed itself when, in order to oppose the Vietnam War, Merry plants a bomb in the local post office that kills a local doctor. Merry then disappears, goes underground, and The Swede spends years looking for her. When he finally tracks her down, she’s back in Newark, New Jersey, living in terrible filth and squalor, and she has converted to a form of ultra-pacifism. She becomes a Jain, J-A-I-N, a religion from India that is so opposed to violence that it refuses to kill even an insect. And The Swede has to contemplate how his beloved daughter could swing from one extreme of murder to this other extreme of pacifism almost beyond reason. The Swede, who’s had this perfect life—sheltered from everything, coasting on inherited prosperity and success on an American dream in a country that has been a golden land for Jews like himself—he has to confront this eruption of what Roth calls “the American berserk,” the country’s capacity to burst out from anybody’s planned order into these forms of strange, bizarre personal violence. Roth is here describing something very real. I mean, I went through, did a quick scroll through incidents that reminded me of the story of Merry Levov—of privileged people, people at every American advantage who lash out, who would adopt some scheme of or some personal ideology of extremist hate, and then lash out in violence against others. There’s so many examples of this. Let me just mention a few that just come to mind in the course of an ordinary search. Remember Elliot Rodger? Elliot Rodger was the son of a Hollywood director. He grew up in very comfortable circumstances. He developed this ideology of misogyny; incel , I think, is the term. Misogyny, violent hatred to women. He killed six people and wounded 14 in a rampage, leaving behind a manifesto justifying what he did. Or Patrick Crusius. He was the man who turned a weapon on a parking lot in El Paso to kill 23 people, motivated by his “Great Replacement,” anti-immigrant ideology. He also acted alone, and he also had a comfortable middle-class upbringing in Dallas, Texas. Or Luigi Mangione—this is a perfect example of this—who comes from a prominent family in Maryland, and he gunned down an insurance executive in New York City. Again, for some crazy, bizarre ideological reason all his own, that unfortunately has found resonance in some of the more malicious corners of online life. Or Ayman Mohamed Ghazali; I’ve talked about him before. He’s the Lebanese immigrant who settled in Michigan, was given the opportunity to make a life for himself in America, given the amazing gift of American citizenship, and instead took guns to Temple Israel in West Bloomfield. You know, these people all have motives. They may be diagnosable as having some kind of mental illness, but they’re not so delusional as not to understand what they’re doing. But they’re acting on some script, some sense of grievance—the American berserk that Roth talks about—that pushes them in these directions. And notice something else. They all have these remarkable resources and freedom. They have the resources to acquire weapons, and they have the freedom to conduct their work without surveillance. There are many societies in which people like this would be caught early because they lived in more of a surveillance state. Americans have freedom, resources. They have the ability to become whoever they are. And for most of us, the ability to become whoever we are is a great gift. It allows us to realize ourselves in all kinds of ways, in ways that people could not realize themselves even in countries that are comparably free but are not as supremely abundant and affluent as the United States. But when you’re given the right to be who you are, that reveals something in some people that is berserk, that is bad. It allows, it gives you more scope to be indulged in wickedness and cruelty and hatefulness, to come up with some crazy set of ideas all your own, or that link in some other way. And to act out against your fellows in ways that bring hurt and harm and sorrow and suffering to the human species. America gives all of us the means to be ourselves, and the question we all face is: Who will we be? That’s it for this week’s episode of The David Frum Show. Thanks so much for watching. As ever, please, the best way to support the work of the show, if you can, is by subscribing to The Atlantic. That helps me and all of my colleagues. Please also consider subscribing to our YouTube channel, or whatever social-media channel you enjoy the program on. Share it with others, and spread the word. See you next week on The David Frum Show. Bye-bye.
